Śramaṇa Daoyan of Wu Commandery.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva (First). His wisdom and virtue are towering;
he is the teacher of the seven Buddhas. A golden lion serves as his seat, and he wears robes of six zhu.
In a previous life, he received a prophecy from Kāśyapa; when his retribution was exhausted, he returned to the Pure Land.
In Sanskrit, Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). He is the teacher of the seven Buddhas of the past.

Within the assembly of Śākyamuni, he manifested in the form of a Bodhisattva to assist in propagating the holy transformation, presiding over all the Bodhisattvas. He is also called a Prince of the Dharma (Dharmarāja-putra).
In the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra*, the Buddha records that Mañjuśrī shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

A verse from the *Mañjuśrīpraṇidhānasūtra* says: "When my life comes to an end, May all obstacles be extinguished; May I behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face And be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Having been born in that Buddha-land, May I fulfill all great vows. May the Tathāgata Amitābha Appear before me and grant me [the prediction of enlightenment]."

I have recorded this: Mañjuśrī was the teacher of the seven Buddhas of the past and has been a Buddha from the very beginning. Nevertheless, his making of vast vows to seek rebirth in Sukhāvatī is like the dance of an eighty-year-old man;
it is for the sake of instructing his children and grandchildren. As the treatise of Nāgārjuna says: "The dance of an octogenarian is for the purpose of teaching his descendants."
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (II):
Compassion arising from the same essence appears in the world; his vows are as deep as the ocean and his conduct as firm as a mountain.
Within a single pore, he traverses lands as numerous as motes of dust, yet still proceeds to the West to behold the countenance of the Sage.

Samantabhadra is also called Pien-chi (Universal Auspiciousness). In the final assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at the Jetavana Grove, he made ten great vows so that all sentient beings throughout the dharma realm might, at the time of their death, be reborn together in Sukhāvatī. The verse says:
"When I am on the verge of passing away, May I completely eliminate all obstacles; May I behold the Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, And immediately attain rebirth in peace."

In that Land of Bliss, once I have been born there, may these great vows be manifested and accomplished before me, fully perfected without exception, bringing benefit and joy to the entire realm of sentient beings.

Although Great-Hearted Bodhisattvas possess wondrous realization of original enlightenment and are suddenly equal to the various Sages, their power and function are as yet not yet sufficient; they have not yet reached the stage where a Tathāgata appears to universally benefit all sentient beings. Therefore—

Only by relying on the World of Ultimate Bliss and drawing near to Amitābha, receiving his prediction of enlightenment, can one manifest countless transformation bodies to universally benefit all realms of sentient beings.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (Third): Excellent!
Samantabhadra is your elder brother; He attained enlightenment countless kalpas ago, And his compassionate vow to deliver sentient beings is inexhaustible.
His name was likewise manifested within the assembly at Weijiang.

Puhui was the younger brother of Puxian; his practices and vows were identical to those of his elder brother. Chan Master Ze of Changlu gathered ten thousand people for the practice of nianfo and established the "Supreme Assembly of the Lotus.
He personally experienced the two Great Bodhisattvas appearing at the assembly to bear witness.
This account is recorded in full in the biography of the Chan Master.
Maitreyanātha Bodhisattva (IV):
Having perfected the Way through samādhi, he descended from beyond; his treatises elucidating Vijñaptimātra are peerless in the world.
Not only did he ascend to Tuṣita during the day, but he further sought to transcend birth and head toward the Land of Bliss.
Maitreyanātha Bodhisattva was a native of Northern India who composed many treatises, including the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Although he ascended to the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven to attend upon Maitreya, he nevertheless authored the *Sukhāvatīvyūhopadeśa*, as well as verses on seeking rebirth in the Pure Land and the Fivefold Method of Practice.
If a person relies upon these to practice with diligence, what doubt could there be that they will transcend this world and proceed to Sukhāvatī?
Ah! Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa (the fifth),
who penetrated the essence and composed this treatise to honor its completion, has manifested profound illumination through his focused mindfulness of Amitābha.
Sentient beings in the five turbidities can give rise to faith; they will certainly transcend [this world] to reach the Land of Bliss and realize non-arising.

Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa was the twelfth patriarch in India. He once composed the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), which elucidates the practice of mindfulness directed toward the Western Land as being most essential.
Having fulfilled the stages of the Three Worthies (*traya-piṭaka*), the Bodhisattva had already entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). As the Buddha prophesied regarding the Dragon...
Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva dwells in the first stage, giving birth to the Pure Land and so forth.
His wondrous functions are boundless as he manifests the Great Middle Way; his treatise is established to refute the schools of existence and non-existence.
The World-Honored One once made a prophecy in the past that the true refuge in Sukhāvatī would first achieve its fruition through Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva.
He was the fourteenth patriarch; a native of South India, after receiving full ordination, he recited and mastered the Tripiṭaka within ninety days.
Having deeply entered into the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), he composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra*, and the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā*.
[The Master] and others frequently praised the Western [Pure Land] and exhorted people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. There is a verse that says:
"If a person aspires to become a Buddha, And mindfully contemplates Amitābha, They shall immediately attain the manifestation of his body; Therefore, I take refuge and pay homage.

If a person wishes to swiftly attain The stage of non-retrogression, They should, with a heart of reverence, Uphold and recite his name. If a person has planted roots of goodness, Yet harbors doubt, then the flower [will not bloom]."

It does not open. For those whose faith is pure, the flower opens and they behold the Buddha. Since even Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas desire to seek birth there, the World-Honored One has made this prophetic declaration;
how can ordinary beings still bound by afflictions rely on anything else but believe?
The Bodhisattva of the Five Supernatural Powers (Seventh),
having accumulated vast merit through inexhaustible deliverance of sentient beings, traveled afar to the West to invite the Buddha;
fifty great-minded followers accompanied the sacred image, and from this point on, the painted likeness spread throughout the Sahā world.
The Bodhisattva Wutong was a monk from the Kukkutapāda Monastery in India. He traveled to the Land of Peace and Bliss to invite Amitābha Buddha, stating:
"The sentient beings of this Sahā world desire to be reborn in the Pure Land, yet they lack the form and countenance of a Buddha; I pray that you deign to descend and grant them your presence."
The Buddha said, "Go on ahead; he shall soon appear there. When the one with the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā) returned, the holy image had already arrived.

A Buddha and fifty bodhisattvas were each seated upon lotus flowers beneath the leaves of trees. The one with the five supernatural powers took note of where the leaves were located, drew the images, and circulated them;
later, they were traced in various colors and distributed throughout the Sahā world. This is recorded in the *Nanshan Lishi Li* (The Annals of the Vinaya Master of the Southern Mountain).
Record of Miraculous Responses from the Three Jewels (Part Eight):
Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu Does Not Leave Mount Lu to Plant White Lotuses;
He Opens a Platform and Establishes a Society to Gather the Multitude of Sages.
Having beheld the Holy Countenance three times upon the Golden Pond, I know that I have a great affinity with Amitābha.

Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin was surnamed Jia and was a native of Yanymen. His learning encompassed both Confucianism and Daoism. When he was over twenty years old, he met Dharma Master Dao’an;
subsequently, while listening to lectures on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he attained sudden and clear enlightenment, exclaiming: "The nine schools differ in their rituals, yet all..."
He was merely like chaff and husks. Later, he entered Mount Lu, where the Regional Inspector Huan Yi established the Donglin Monastery for him to reside in.
For thirty years, his shadow never left the mountain; whenever he saw a guest off, he used Tiger Creek as the boundary.

At that time, Liu Yimin, Lei Cizong, and seventeen others followed Huiyuan in their travels and stayed there. They gathered one hundred and twenty-three people to form the Lotus Society. Huiyuan, at...

He performed the ritual recitations of the Pure Land at the six periods of the day with diligent perseverance and without retreat. After ten years, he beheld the sacred form of Amitābha three times upon the golden pond.
Nineteen years later, on the evening of the last day of the seventh month, as he arose from meditative concentration at the Prajñā Terrace, he saw the body of Buddha Amitābha filling the void;
within his circular halo were various transformation Buddhas, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance to his left and right.
Furthermore, he saw the light of flowing water divided into fourteen streams, pouring upward and downward, proclaiming "suffering" and "emptiness.
The Buddha told Yuan: "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you. Seven days from now, you shall be born in my land."
He further saw Buddhabhadra, Huichi, and Tanshun by the Buddha’s side. They came forward and bowed to Huiyuan, saying, "Master, your aspirations preceded ours;
why have you arrived so late? Thereafter, they said to their disciples, "When I first resided here, I was fortunate enough to behold the holy countenance of the Buddha three times in the Pure Land.
Now I have seen it once more; my rebirth there is certain. Seven days later, he indeed passed away.

The disciples escorted his remains for burial on the Western Ridge. Xie Lingyun composed an inscription, and Zhang Ye wrote a preface. During the Great Song dynasty, he was posthumously titled Grand Master Yuanwu (Great Enlightenment).
His miscellaneous writings, totaling ten fascicles, are known as the *Lushan Collection* and circulate in the world. The Master is regarded as the founding patriarch of the Lotus Society.
Dharma Master Huizhi (the ninth):
Having severed the cords of attachment, his will is set upon the Western Land; his measure is profound and deep, the fragrance of his realization of the Way spreads afar.
As elder brother, he joined the same religious society with me; like the alternating sounds of the *xuan* and *chi* flutes, their harmonies resound long and clear.
Dharma Master Huizhi was the younger brother of Master Huiyuan. His character was profound and his spirit was brilliant and refined.

Together with his elder brother, he formed the Lotus Society with one hundred and twenty-three people. One day, he took leave of his brother to enter Shu; Huiyuan tried to detain him, but could not prevail.

He sighed, saying, "Human life loves to gather; you alone delight in separation. Hōchi replied, "If one were to remain attached to the emotion of gathering, one should not have left the household life in the first place.
Now that I have severed my attachments to seek the Way, I am taking the Western Land as my destination. Thereupon, they parted with mutual regret.
My late elder brother had already attained rebirth there.
Dharma Master Daozhen (X):
Having passed away at Mount Lu, he has distanced himself from the dust and grime; the cliffs and valleys shine as brightly as rows of torches lit.
Having just left the five sufferings, he shall finally behold the Buddha; what need is there for a golden platform to come and welcome him?

Dharma Master Daozhen of the Liang dynasty stayed at Mount Lu during the Tianjian era. Hearing that this was the site where Master Huiyuan had formerly established a society for pure cultivation, he felt deep admiration for it.
However, his initial resolve remained hesitant. Later, he suddenly dreamed that dozens of people on the sea were rowing a boat forward.
Daozhen asked where they were going; they replied, "We are heading to the Land of Amitābha. Daozhen said, "I wish..."
[The Master] asked, "Will you be able to go as you wish? He replied, "With your intention, who would dare refuse you?
However, the merit of one day’s practice here surpasses that of eternal kalpas. You have not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*; how can you seek to go there?

Later, Zhenjue sighed with shame, thinking, "If I were to have any discrepancy regarding the Holy Dharma. Thereupon, he devoted himself exclusively to reciting this sūtra. Two years later, suddenly his hall became empty.
At the door, someone appeared holding a silver platform and said, "Dharma Master, when your retribution is exhausted, you shall ascend this platform.

He added, "The meritorious conduct of the Master should have caused you to ride upon a golden platform; why then do you remain hesitant in your initial resolve? This is precisely why [the silver platform has come].

Fazhen thanked him, saying, "If I am indeed able to transcend the three realms and escape the five sufferings, then my foundation for seeing the Buddha will gradually be established. Why must it necessarily be..."

"Is this the Golden Terrace? On the evening of Zhen’s passing, the cliffs and valleys were filled with a brilliant light, as if a thousand torches were shining together. The local villagers were struck with wonder.
When dawn broke, they went to the mountain to investigate and thus learned that this was the verification of Zhen’s death and his rebirth in the Pure Land.
Dharma Master Tanyuan (11):
Casting aside the texts of the immortals, he received the *Amitābha Sūtra*; how can longevity compare to studying the birthless?
Chanting the Buddha’s name in unison as he passed away, celestial music was played in the sky by day to welcome him.
Dharma Master Tanluan of the Later Wei was a native of Yanmen. In his youth, he traveled to Mount Wutai; moved by its spiritual wonders, he subsequently sought to leave the secular life.

He was able to peruse the scriptures of the Three Vehicles, yet by nature he was fond of esoteric arts. Hearing that Tao Yuanming, the Hermit of Jiangnan, possessed methods for longevity, he traveled a thousand *li* to seek him out.
Tao immediately bestowed upon him ten fascicles of the *Xianjing* (Cinnabar Scripture); Tanluan rejoiced, deeming it divine.
The attainment of immortals can certainly be achieved. Later, he returned to Luoyang and encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci. He asked, "Does the Buddhist path include longevity?
Bodhiruci sighed and said, "Longevity and immortality—these are the teachings of our Buddha. What could the Daoist school possibly possess of them?"

He then presented the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* to him, saying, "You should recite this; practice according to its instructions, and you shall leave the defiled land to take up residence in a pure realm, where your lifespan will be immeasurable and you shall attain all supreme and wondrous merits. Tanyou deeply believed his words;

he subsequently burned the immortal scriptures and devoted himself exclusively to the *Contemplation Sutra*. He did not flag despite the cold, heat, or illness. One day, while he was correctly holding [the text]...
During his recitation, a Brahman monk suddenly entered the room and said, "I am Nāgārjuna. Because you possess a mind for the Pure Land, I have come to see you from that realm.
Daoluan asked, "How shall you instruct me? Nāgārjuna replied, "The past has gone and cannot be reached;
the future has not yet arrived and cannot be pursued. Where is the present? It is as difficult to turn back the white horse [of time] as it is to catch it. Having spoken these words, he vanished.
Fah-luan, perceiving that his death was imminent due to these extraordinary signs, immediately gathered the assembly to instruct them, commanding them to chant the name of Amitābha Buddha aloud.
Fah-luan then faced west, closed his eyes, and passed away. The entire assembly simultaneously heard the sounds of pipes, strings, and flutes coming from the west; after a long while, they ceased.
The Great Zen Master Si of Nanyue (12):
His traces of zazen on Mount Heng still remain; the form of Amitābha appeared in his dreams, making the Way even more sublime.
Do not say that he has departed without transforming sentient beings—he has swallowed the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time with a single mouth.
Later, there was the Chan Master Huisi of the Northern Zhou dynasty. He was a native of Wujin and surnamed Li. A fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) grew upon his crown.

One night, he dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the household life; Huisi then took leave of his parents to enter the Way. Upon receiving full ordination, he practiced seated meditation daily and maintained the practice of eating only once a day.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and other scriptures until he had completed one thousand full repetitions. Hearing that Master Huìwén of the Northern Qi had several hundred disciples and that his Way was flourishing, he went there to seek the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
After twenty-one days, he attained the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajñāna*) and realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

At that time, while residing at Mount Nanyue, he practiced the *Vaipulya-prāyaścitta* (the Ritual of Repentance for the Vaipulya Sūtras) and made a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land. In a dream, he was moved by Amitābha’s preaching.
The Dharma. Thereupon, the Chen Emperor repeatedly extended his consolations and honors. As the Great Chan Master was about to pass away, he said to his disciples:
"You must not spare your own lives; you should constantly practice the Lotus Sūtra, the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddha-remembrance samādhi, and the Vaipulya repentance rites.
Impermanence is swift; each of you should exert yourselves. The Master passed away with serene composure. A wondrous fragrance filled the chamber, and his countenance—
Shè (Color/Form) was like his birth; Sī (Thought) remained throughout his life. Someone once exhorted him, saying, "Why do you not go down the mountain to transform and deliver sentient beings?
The Master replied, "The Buddhas of the three periods have been swallowed by me in a single mouth; where else could there be any sentient beings to be transformed?
Such was the Master’s functional mastery. His disciples who received the Dharma from him were very numerous, but it was only the Great Master Zhìzhě of Tiantái who propagated [the teachings].
Chanjiao said: "I enlarge my family’s legacy with these words. Hui-ming Chan Master (13):
Nanyue and Qixin pay homage at the Buddha niche, vowing to become fellow practitioners in the Pure Land.
In a single morning, he joined his palms like a cicada shedding its skin; who would say that both were eighty-three years old?
Master Huiming had a profound mastery of the teachings and practiced meditative contemplation for a long time.

Together with Master Nanyue Huisi, he performed the Vaipulya Repentance Rite, both vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land. At the moment of his death, he sat in the full lotus position facing west and cried out, "The Buddha is coming!"
With palms joined, he passed away. Both were eighty-three years old. At that time, people saw celestial banners and streamers and cried out, "Excellent!
They have come to welcome you," as they departed. Chan Master Jing’ai (14).
I vow to extract my entrails and pull out my lungs, that my aspiration may be boundless; My resolve for the Dharma is as firm as iron and stone.
May I cast off this defiled body to be born in the Pure Land, Where a single flower shall bloom before the Awakened King.
Master Jing’ai was by nature stern and resolute, devoting himself solely to the principles of Chan meditation. Because Emperor Wu suppressed Buddhism, Jing’ai lamented his own lack of power.
Hufa addressed his disciples, saying: "I have brought no benefit to the world; I shall now relinquish this body.

He then severed his own hands and feet and laid them upon a stone, hung his intestines and stomach from the branches of a tree, and after cutting out his heart and holding it up, he passed away. He further composed a verse to show the assembly, saying:
"Abandoning this defiled form, I vow to be born in the Pure Land. At the blooming of a flower in a single thought, may I reach the presence of Amitābha Buddha."
Chan Master Sengya (15): Having sought the Way for many years, he awakened to the Mahayana; How could it have been difficult for him to burn his five fingers?
At the end of his life, flowers rained down from the heavens in countless numbers; Six hundred monks followed one after another as he ascended toward the West.
Chan Master Sengya resided at Duobao Monastery in Yizhou, where his Way was widely practiced.

Once, at the west of the city, he burned his upper and lower fifth fingers as an offering to the Three Holy Ones of the Pure Land. Over one hundred thousand monastics and laypeople gathered around him.
When someone asked if it pained him, he replied, "Since my mind has no pain, how could my fingers be pained? He then said to his disciples: "After my parinirvāṇa..."
"You should serve the sick and the ugly with diligence. For such individuals as these are mostly great-minded bodhisattvas manifesting through skillful means;
were it not for one’s realization of the principle of equality, how could one show them universal respect?

At the time of his passing, he saw celestial flowers falling like rain; clad in a patchwork robe and holding a mendicant’s staff, he ascended into the air with six hundred monks and vanished toward the west.
The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai (16):
The wondrous Threefold Contemplation within a single mind is difficult to conceive; Yet even the Pure Land can be discussed through the Ten Doubts.
Sitting or reclining facing west, never changing until the end, At the fragrant altar and jeweled trees, there shall be a time of return.
The Great Master Zhizhe of the Chen Dynasty was named Zhiyi. He was a native of Huarong in Jingzhou and belonged to the secular Chen clan.

At his birth, there were manifold auspicious omens, and in his youth he possessed extraordinary features; his skin did not retain impurities. At the age of seven, he entered Guoyuan Temple and heard a monk reciting the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*;
he immediately began to recite it along with him, suddenly remembering the text of all seven fascicles as if it were already familiar to him.
Due to his past conditioning, at fifteen he prostrated before a Buddha image and vowed to leave the household life. At eighteen, he followed the monastic lineage of Guoyuan and received the tonsure.
At twenty, he received full ordination. In the first year of the Tianjia era, he visited Master Huisi of Dasu Mountain in Guangzhou.
Upon seeing him, Huisi said, "In the past, we listened to the Lotus Sutra together on Vulture Peak; now you have come here once again. He then showed him the practice of Samantabhadra.

At the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he preached the four modes of peaceful conduct. The Master entered meditative observation for twenty-one days. His latent spiritual penetrations manifested secretly;
he alone understood them clearly. He reported his realization to Si, who said: "What you have realized is something that none but I can recognize.
This is the *Sūtra-alaṃkāra-dhāraṇī* of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Even if there were a million masters of doctrinal study, they could not exhaust your eloquence. You may..."

"Transmit the Lamp! Do not become one who severs the seed of the Buddha for the last time. In the first year of the Dajian era, he took his leave of Master Si and departed for Jinling to propagate the teachings.
Whenever he preached the Dharma, he did not rely on written texts; through his wondrous eloquence, he was entirely without impediment.

In the seventh year, he sent his disciples to Mount Fulong at Tiantai, where Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty had established a Chan residence and allotted tax revenues to provide for the community's expenses.
Upon reaching the Sui dynasty, Emperor Yang invited the Master to receive the Bodhisattva Precepts from him and bestowed upon him the title "Zhizhe" (Wise One).
The Master constantly wore a single tattered robe as he traveled between Tiantai for over twenty years.

He categorized and interpreted the entirety of the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his lifetime according to the Five Periods and Eight Teachings, and revealed the essential meaning of the Perfect and Sudden One-Mind Three-Contemplations. Furthermore, he established monasteries, cast images, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks.
His number was beyond counting. He was resolute in his devotion to the Western Land and exhorted others to advance in their practice. He authored the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*).

Although many masters throughout the successive dynasties have produced works concerning the Pure Land, none surpass this book in its ultimate essence and subtlety. When the Master was approaching death, he burned incense, took up his brush, and composed the *Verses on Contemplating the Mind*.
He ordered his disciples to chant the names of the Sixteen Contemplations and instructed the assembly, saying: "The Forty-eight..."
I vow to adorn and purify the Buddha-land. Its fragrant terraces and jewel-trees are easily reached by those who have no one to rely upon.

Even those for whom the signs of the burning-wheels of hell appear can still attain rebirth if they repent in a single thought. The power of practicing the Way shall never be in vain; the Brahma-sound shall never deceive anyone.

Having spoken these words, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. He was sixty years of age. His miraculous deeds were numerous, as detailed in his original biography. Dhyāna Master Daoyu (17):
Carving a Tathāgata from a three-inch sandalwood block, To fill the entirety of empty space—how truly extraordinary!
"If the Buddha manifests according to one's mind, even within a thicket of thorns, the *juehua* (bodhi-flower) shall bloom.
Master Daoyu of Sui dynasty left the household life at Kaijue Temple. He had deep faith in the Pure Land and recited the name of Amitābha Buddha.
He fashioned a sandalwood image three inches in height. Later, he suddenly died; after seven days, he revived and said, "I went to the Western Land and saw Amitābha Buddha, who said to me:
'You have fashioned my image; why is it so small? I replied: 'If the mind is great, the image is great; if the mind is small, the image is small.
Having spoken, the image filled the entirety of space, and [the Buddha] declared: 'Return now to your original place.'"

In her home country, she bathed in fragrant water. At the moment the morning star appeared, she said, "I shall come to welcome you. When the appointed time arrived, she was indeed met by a transformed Buddha who came to welcome her;
his radiance illuminated the room, and she immediately passed away. This occurred in the eighth year of the Kaihuang era.
Master Hong (18): Having already firmly maintained the characteristics of the Vinaya, how much more so for those in the West who race toward the daily recitation;
though not born in the Inner Court, they are born in the Pure Land—how many people can truly understand this mind?
Dharma Master Hong was a native of Bingzhou. Throughout his life, he cultivated the practice of purity; he would not take money or precious objects in his hands.

When the time of his death approached, he saw boys and girls from Tuṣita Heaven coming to welcome him. Hong said, "I have set my expectation upon the Western Land; I shall not be reborn in the heavens.

He then instructed his disciples to recite the Buddha's name, saying aloud, "The Buddha of the Western Land has come to welcome me. Having finished speaking, he passed away. This occurred during the reign of Emperor Renzong.
In his fourth year,
Dharma Master Deng (19) ascended the lion throne and lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; his disciples gathered around him, all filled with joy.
He exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing; the clouds of incense pervading the world could truly be beheld by those with faith.

As for Dharma Master Deng, he had a profound understanding of the scriptural teachings. While lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Xingguo Monastery in Bingzhou, both monastics and laypeople came to listen;
whether old or young, he led them all to orally recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, exhorting them to be reborn there together.

On the evening of his passing in the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era, a rare fragrance welcomed him. At the time of his enshrinement, radiant light and fragrant clouds pervaded the entire region of Jiu Luo.
After Master Daochuo (20) finished lecturing on the *Contemplation Sūtra*, he sat upon his square couch; As Shandao assisted him, his virtuous practice became even more manifest.
In response to his prior invocation of the Buddha’s words, at the moment of his passing, The three paths of light from the white tuft of hair shone toward the east.

When Meditation Master Daocuo resided in Xihe, he lectured daily on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* and cultivated samādhi through practice. He personally drilled gourd-seed beads (*huazhu*) and exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name.
He once had Shan Dao lead him into meditative absorption to observe whether he would attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

The Buddha declared that on the day Daocuo passed away, a ray of light from the white tuft between his brows would shine far toward the east; when this light appears, one shall come to be born in my land. Indeed, it was so.
On the day Chō passed away, the white tuft of hair on his forehead radiated light throughout the room.
It is clear that the Brahma-voice of the Buddha never deceives anyone. Master Shandao (21).
The practice of Buddha-remembrance flourished extensively throughout Chang’an; with every word uttered, a radiance shone forth.
Copying scriptures and painting murals were inconceivable acts that provided inexhaustible provisions to aid rebirth in the Pure Land.
Shandao of the Tang dynasty—though his origins are unknown—met Master Chao of Xihé during the Zhenguan era and received the *Jiupin daochang jing* (The Scripture on the Nine Grades of Rebirth).

On one occasion, while lecturing on the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, Daohui said, "This is truly the essential gateway for entering the Buddha’s way. Cultivating other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish;
only this gate of visualization allows for the swift transcendence of birth and death. Thereupon, he constantly applied himself with diligent effort.

Whenever he entered the Buddha chamber to recite the Buddha’s name, he knelt upright with palms joined, never ceasing until his strength was exhausted. Even on days of bitter cold, he would continue to flow [with devotion].
Hàn continued to travel to the capital, where he transformed the fourfold assembly for over thirty years. Those who recited the Buddha’s name were beyond counting.
He provided offerings for the transcription of more than one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and had over three hundred walls painted with illustrations of the Pure Land.
Whenever the Master himself recited the Buddha’s name even once, a ray of light would issue from his mouth.
From ten up to a hundred times, the light appeared in this same manner. Later, he said to others, "This body is loathsome; all things are subject to suffering and change.

He then climbed a tall willow tree and, facing west, made this vow: "May the Buddha receive me; may the Bodhisattvas assist me, so that I do not lose right mindfulness and do not fall back into regression.
Having spoken, he threw himself down and ended his life. Tradition holds that Shao Kang was none other than this monk.
The Body of the Dharma: Chan Master Zhao (22). Five Assemblies:
Conditions Arising, Moving Five Clouds; the Buddha’s Voice Resounds from Afar, Reaching the Imperial Palace.
Had he not received Manjusri’s instruction in those years, how could he have attained such wondrous perfuming through kalpas?
Chan Master Fazhao established a five-assembly *nianfo* dharma hall at Hudong Temple in Hengzhou in the fourth year of the Dali era.
He was moved by the appearance of auspicious clouds of five colors covering the temple; within the clouds were towers and pavilions, and there he beheld Amitabha Buddha and...
The two bodhisattvas were of immense stature, filling the entirety of space. Later, when Daozhao went to Mount Wutai, he saw them in the lecture hall of Zhulin Monastery.
Mañjuśrī was on the west and Samantabhadra was on the east, preaching the Dharma to the assembly. Daozhao then prostrated himself and said:
"In this degenerate age, ordinary beings possess shallow knowledge and meager wisdom; thus, the Buddha-nature within the mind-ground has no means by which it may manifest. Unfinished.
[Zhao] inquired, "Which Dharma gate is most essential? Mañjuśrī replied, "Regarding what you have asked, now is precisely the right time.

Among all gates of practice, none is equal to the mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Because I, in the past, practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha, I attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Zhao asked again, "How should one practice this mindfulness? Mañjuśrī said, "To the west of this world, there is Amitābha..."
"The Buddha’s power of vows is inconceivable. You should fix your mindfulness upon it and not allow it to be interrupted; at the time of death, you will certainly be reborn there.
Having said this, he stroked [Daoxuan’s] head with his hand and withdrew. Thereupon, he came to Bingzhou and widely exhorted people to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Emperor Dezong frequently heard the sound of the recitation of the Buddha’s name coming from the northeast within the palace. He dispatched an envoy to search for its source, which led him to Dakang.

Observing the flourishing success of his exhortations and conversions, he returned to the capital to report this. By imperial decree, he was invited into the palace to teach the nuns to recite the Buddha's name;
he also established the Five Assemblies. (Master Shaokang, twenty-third)
From this time forth, Amitābha, the Great Teacher, With a single coin and a single thought, entices the multitude of children.
His transformation spreads through Xin and Ding as vast as the distant void; How many wandering beings ascend the precious pool!
Master Shaokang was a native of Xiandu in Jinyun. At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he arrived at Baima Temple in Luoyang. There, he beheld the temple hall...

The characters within repeatedly emitted light. Upon examining them, it was found to be the text on the Western Paradise composed by Master Shandao for the purpose of guiding beings toward rebirth there.
Jingkong said, "If I have a karmic affinity with the Pure Land, may this text emit light once more. Before he had finished speaking, the light flashed again.
Jingkong declared, "Though kalpa-stones may be worn away, my vow shall never change. Thereupon, he proceeded to the portrait of Master Shandao in Chang’an.

In the hall, while he was arranging the remains of the offerings, he suddenly saw the deceased master’s portrait rise into the air. The portrait said to him, "Rely upon me and serve [the Dharma] to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

By virtue of your merit, we shall be reborn together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Furthermore, on the road he encountered a monk who said, "If you wish to transform others, you should go to Xin-ding, which is the present-day Yan-zhou.
When you arrive there, people will not recognize you; therefore, take money with you. Upon reaching that place, no one recognized him, so he used the money...
He enticed small children, saying, "Amitābha Buddha is your original teacher; if you recite his name once, I will give you one coin.
After more than a month had passed and many were waiting for the coins, Kang said, "You may now recite ten times and receive one coin.
Thus, for a year, people—whether young or old, noble or humble—who recited the Buddha’s name filled the roads. He then established a Pure Land [temple] on Mount Oryong.

At the Earthly Dharma-Altar (Tudaochang), he constructed a three-tiered altar. He gathered the assembly at midnight to perform the ritual practice. Kang would chant "Buddha" in a loud voice, and the assembly would join him in unison.

Whenever Master Kang uttered the sound of "Buddha," the assembly saw a Buddha emerge from his mouth, appearing like a string of pearls. Kang said, "Those of you who see the Buddha will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, there were some who did not see it at all. When Kang was approaching the end of his life, he emitted light several times.
The Way vanished in an instant.
Master Kuiji of Cien (24): His school propagated the path of Cien;
the claim that the three carts followed behind him is but a hollow legend.
"Amida Tongzan" provides skillful means; when the period of retribution is fulfilled, one is ultimately entrusted to the nine lotuses.
Master Kuiji’s surname was Wei-chi. He was a native of Dai-jun and the nephew of Jing-de. From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and noble-minded;
having read the scriptures, commentaries, and records but once, he could recite them from memory. Tripitaka Master Xuanzang requested that he leave the household life, whereupon...

He entered the Way as a monk and received the core teachings of Yogācāra and Vijñaptimātra from Xuanzang. He authored approximately one hundred treatises, earning him the title "Master of the Hundred Treatises.

He once composed the *Praise of Universal Amitābha*, which elucidates the essential meaning of the Western Paradise and exhorts people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and cultivate the Pure Land.
Some say that his character was extravagant; he was constantly followed by wine, meat, and women in three carriages. This is how he was characterized.
It is said that the Dharma Master Sanche [was the founder]. Zanning, the Chief Administrator of Monks (*Sengtong*), in his *History of the Sangha* (*Sengshi*), vehemently refutes this claim.
The single school of Cien still exists to this day. (Master Huaiyu, No. 25)
The True Realm of the Surging Spring belongs to Tiantai; in the long-sitting pine-cabin, he was cut off from all coming and going.
He recited the Sacred Scriptures three hundred thousand times, and when he was invited back, he directly attained the Purple-Golden Terrace.

Dharma Master Huaiyu was a native of Taizhou. He upheld the Vinaya with such rigorous integrity that his reputation for high character was sharp and prominent. He lived on coarse food and distributed [his alms] to others.
He sat upright for long periods without reclining. Daily, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha fifty thousand times and chanted the *Amitābha Sūtra* three hundred thousand scrolls.
One day, he suddenly beheld a multitude of holy beings from the West, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Among them was one person holding a silver platform who entered through a window. The man said, "I wish to obtain a golden platform to attain rebirth thereupon," and then vanished. This was [the account of] Yu.
He redoubled his diligent efforts. Later, he heard a voice in the air saying, "There is a halo above the Master's head; please sit in the full lotus posture and form the mudrā.
At that moment, Buddhas filled the room. He then spoke a verse and passed away with a smile.
Master Ying (26): Carrying volumes of scripture with you, never casting them aside for even a moment—seeking out texts and verifying meanings is but a weary toil.
If you wish in the future to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it would be better to turn your mind and fix your mindfulness upon the High One.
The Dharma Master Ying resided in the Eastern Capital and lectured on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra forty times. Thereupon, he entered the meditation hall of Master Chuo and deeply penetrated into samādhi.
He then sighed, saying, "I regret that for many years I have merely sought out textual commentaries, only exhausting my body and mind.
Why not instead aspire to the inconceivable power of Buddha-remembrance? He subsequently exerted himself in the pure practices and ultimately returned to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
Master Yan (27): Daochuo bestowed his compassion by lecturing on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*; in the midst of ordinary life, the moon of the mind suddenly shone bright.
Having focused single-mindedly on Amitābha Buddha for five years, he immediately attained the ability to walk upon the golden ground.

Dharma Master Yan encountered Meditation Master Chao of Xihe while he was lecturing on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. Only then did he come to understand the dharma-gate of contemplating the mind through the mindfulness of the Buddha.
He subsequently abandoned literary studies, established a practice hall, and performed a thousand prostrations daily, single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha.
After five years of diligent practice, he passed away and was reborn in the Pure Land.
The monk Weian (28) gazed upon the two sages with his own eyes;
indeed, they were most extraordinary. He further recorded their compassionate countenances and had them depicted in a painting.
"O youth, I vow to follow you back to the Pure Land. Before the image, he bathed with incense and sat in the full lotus posture.

Wei An was a native of Bingzhou. He specialized in the cultivation of wondrous contemplation. Upon emerging from samādhi, the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta appeared in the air and did not vanish for a long time.
Wei An prostrated himself, weeping and sighing, saying: "By the grace of my physical eyes, I have been able to behold the Holy Ones."
Yong lamented that he regretted there would be no one in later generations to transmit his work. Suddenly, two men appeared who called themselves painters;
before their arms had even been extended, the sacred images were completed, yet the two men vanished. Yuan’an said, "My journey to the West is now the time for this."
"Among my disciples, there may be those who would follow me; you should speak of this clearly. A young boy said, "I wish to follow my teacher.
Hui'an said, "If you can truly follow me, you must go home and inform your parents. When his parents heard this, they laughed and scolded him.

The boy then returned to the temple, bathed himself with incense water, and sat in the *paryaṅka* (lotus) posture before the statue of Amitābha Buddha and departed. Hui’an immediately burned incense before the image, took up a brush, and wrote:
The verse has also passed (yi). Sengweigong (29):
Wine-bibbers and gambling companions meet daily; His conduct was modeled after Lingkui, and everyone mocked him.
That he did not fall into hell was not due to his own power, but solely because the Great Awakened One’s King of Vows was exalted—this I revere.
At Mount Jia’s Faxon Temple in Jingzhou, he was arrogant toward those above and swallowed those below; he befriended those of improper character.

Yet, when he had occasional leisure, he would lecture on and recite the scriptures, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). Nevertheless, wine-bibbers and gambling companions filled his chambers daily.

The temple monk Lingkui’s conduct was modeled after his [the Master’s]. The people of Jingzhou mocked him in jest, saying: "Lingkui has committed every possible transgression; weiweng follows in his footsteps.
Though there are thousands of layers of hell, do not grow weary of being the first to enter. When Weigong heard this, he said: "Since I have already created karma, how can I deny it?
However, I rely on the Teacher of the Western Land to pity my faults and pull me from the mire and ashes."
In the second year of the Qianning era, Senggong died, though no one yet knew it.

Sengyuei went a hundred paces outside the monastery when he encountered six or seven young men on the road, dressed in colorful garments and holding musical instruments as if they belonged to a Kucha troupe. He asked them where they were coming from.
The youths replied, "We come from the West. He then asked, "Where does the Venerable Senggong reside? Sengyuei pointed the way out for them. From within their robes, the youths...
He brought forth a golden pitcher. From within the pitcher, he took a lotus flower; it was as closed as a fist, but gradually it blossomed until its petals were as large as bowls.
From beneath each petal, light radiated in succession, streaming toward the temple. Dao Kui was greatly startled and could not turn back to look.
The next day, when Dao Kui returned to the temple, he heard the sound of the bells and saw the monks all gathered at the gate. He then said:
Wang Gong was about to die at evening. On the night of his death, a monk in the temple dreamed that the radiance of a lotus flower appeared in his room and departed after a long while.
Thereupon, Wang Kui was moved to realization; he subsequently maintained his integrity and virtue, becoming a man of lofty character.
Dharma Master Huai-gan (30):
Already knowing that Shandao was his true teacher, He sought rebirth in the Pure Land with unwavering faith.
Desiring to enlighten future generations, he composed this treatise; At the moment of death, he joined his palms and turned westward.

Dharma Master Huai-gan resided at Qianfu Monastery in Chang’an. Following the exhortation of Master Shandao—who told him that if he could single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, he would surely receive personal verification—he subsequently established a seven-times-seven-day (twenty-one day) ritual site. Yet, no response had yet been received.

Regretting his own deep transgressions, he wished to fast until death; however, Shandao stopped him and would not permit it. For three years he practiced with single-minded devotion, whereupon he beheld the Buddha’s golden countenance and jade-like *ūrṇā-kośa*.
He then attained *samādhi* and composed the *Wǎngshēng juéyì lùn* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning Rebirth) in seven fascicles.
He universally exhorted the fourfold assembly to cultivate this Dharma gate. At the time of his death, the Buddha came to welcome him, and he passed away with palms joined.
Master Zhilian (XXXI): With body and mind pure and upright, he takes the Way as his reliance; though possessing a mouth, how could he ever discuss right or wrong?
Being distinct in the ultimate sense from both cessation and arising, the Land of Lotus Flowers is his true home.

The Master’s name was Zhilian. His nature was pure and steadfast; he would not allow matters of right and wrong to linger on his lips. He traveled extensively to consult venerable elders, pursuing the Way with great urgency.
Nevertheless, he focused his mind single-mindedly on the Western Pure Land. At the age of eighty-two, being free from illness, he wrote this verse:

“The wild geese pass through the vast sky, Their shadows sink into the cold waters. Neither extinguished nor born— Within the land of the lotus flowers. The following morning at dawn, he announced [his passing].
The assembly said, "I have already seen Amitābha Buddha. His body is eight feet tall, with a golden complexion and a jade-like ūrṇā-kośa.

Surrounded by a multitude from the ocean [of assemblies], he preached the Dharma, saying: 'All you superior and virtuous people, you should give rise to great faith, cultivate all wholesome dharmas, and come to be born in my land.
Having finished speaking, he immediately vanished. Since I have seen the Buddha, my rebirth there is certain. Having spoken thus, he turned his body toward...
He passed away lying on his right side facing west. Master Zang (32):
Diligent in the six mindfulnesses, the Way was perfected; indeed, at the very end, he beheld the radiant light.
The various devas played music as they all came from the void; a manifested Buddha arrived to welcome him, and he immediately set forth on his journey.

Master Zang of the Chan school was a native of Fenzhou. In his youth, he traveled throughout the four quarters, paying homage at pagodas and temples. Until his old age, he did not accept prostrations from either monastics or laypeople.
His mind was sincere and his practice arduous; he never forgot the Pure Land. On the day of his passing, the various devas played music.

Successive manifestations of welcoming buddhas arrived, yet he declined to go with them all. Finally, when the transformation Buddha from the West came to welcome him, he took his leave of the assembly and departed. Sengtanjian (33):
Within samādhi, Amitābha washes his heart; A lotus appears within the vase, moved by his profound sincerity.
He raised his voice to chant the name as he walked through the city walls. [At that time,] Tanjian, a native of Jiangling, was listening to the Dharma sounds at the incense altar above.
He had always vowed that his body would ascend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss to behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face;
thus, even when performing a single hair’s breadth of merit, he dedicated it toward the adornment of the Pure Land. One day, while in meditative concentration, the Buddha sprinkled water upon him.
Faren said, "Wash away your defilements and purify your thoughts. He then drew a lotus flower from his flask and gave it to him.
Emerging from samādhi, he took leave of the monks of the monastery. Deep into the night, he paced the cloister, chanting the Buddha's name with a resolute voice.
At dawn, he greeted the assembly as usual, sat cross-legged, and passed away in tranquility.
Chan Master Daxing (34): Eating pine needles and wearing lotus robes, he seeks nothing outside; He refines his cultivation of the Lotus Samādhi even further.
The lapis lazuli ground appears, opening the eye of the mind; The Tathāgatas of the three periods smile and nod their heads.
Dachang Chanshi was a native of Qizhou. He entered Mount Tai to live in grass garments and subsist on wood and water, practicing the Lotus Samādhi.

Moved by his devotion, Samantabhadra manifested before him to instruct him in the recitation of the Buddha's name. After twenty-one days had passed, at about midnight, he suddenly saw a ground of lapis lazuli.
His spiritual eye opened and became clear; he beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions and then passed away on his right side. A wondrous fragrance did not dissipate for several days.
When Dharma Master Da’ang (35) finished his lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*, Dao Yuan attained realization, and music descended directly from the sky to welcome him.
"In the celestial realms, there is birth and there is death; how can they compare to the Pure Land where one realizes the path of non-birth?
Dharma Master Ang was lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* in Xiangzhou when he heard the sounds of a multitude coming from the sky.
They announced: "This is Tuṣita Heaven; we have come down specifically to welcome you. Ang replied: "The heavenly realm is the very root of birth and death. I have never [sought it]."
"I vow that when I reach the Western Land I aspire to, if music and dancers come from the west to welcome me, I shall go there.
Having finished these words, the incense burner fell from his hand; he sat upright upon his high seat and departed.
The Assembly’s *Vina* (36): Transmitted from the Liang Dynasty, how could these words be mere empty flattery? Seeking birth in the Pure Land is fundamentally not difficult;
by reciting the Buddha's name at the moment of death, one transcends to rebirth. A single grain of elixir transforms iron into gold.
Regarding the assembly of the *karmadāna*: A person from Su served as a monastic administrator (*gaṅwei*) for many members at Wanshou Chan Temple.

When he fell ill and was near death, he twice requested the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name using the funds from his robes and alms bowl. After he passed away, it was time for the evening session (*fangcan*) to begin in the communal quarters.

I heard from atop the beam that the *karmadāna* Ji had been born in the Pure Land. The assembly in the hall was struck with alarm and wondered how he could have attained birth there when they suspected he lacked pure karma.
A short while later, the voice from the beam spoke again: "At the time of his death, he twice requested the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name; therefore, he attained rebirth.
Observing the case of the *karmadāna* Ji, it is clear that for people of the world to request others to recite the Buddha’s name at the moment of death is truly an essential path.
[From] the *Baozhu ji* (Collection of Jewels).
Dharma Master Xiānzhāng (37): His teachings and contemplations were comprehensive and penetrating, and his virtuous deeds were preeminent; people called him "Tiger Cub," for whom there was no peer.
He left his seat in the Dharma Hall in the lotus posture and vowed not to rise until he had secured the Golden Terrace;

thus did Master Xianzhang set an example. His name was Zhongmin; he was a native of Sanqu. From his youth, he mastered both the Mahayana and Hinayana scriptures, earning him the nickname "The Tiger Cub" within the Garden of the Teachings.
Later, he presided over Fushi Monastery. He once spoke with great confidence, saying: "In my assembly, there shall be no fewer than five hundred followers."
Consequently, he did not lecture on the Mahāyāna sūtras, as he was unable to fulfill his own words; thus, throughout his life, he lectured only on the Hīnayāna texts.
Upon reaching the conclusion of his commentary, he hurried back to Benye Monastery, gathered the great assembly in the Dharma Hall, and ascended the lion throne.

Just as he sat cross-legged, he suddenly saw a silver platform from the West arrive through the air. He then proclaimed: "Throughout my life, I have understood the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); I vow to attain..."
Why should rebirth on the Golden Terrace not be possible? Closing one's eyes at the end—this is how it is done.
Monk Zhìtōng (38): Refining his practice in the Pure Land, he looked up to the sages of old;
In ritual and observance he was according to the Dharma, following the teachings of Cí'ān.
Lotus flowers open and close as auspicious birds gather; this is the manifestation of the Western Realm before one's eyes.
Zhitong of Zhixiang was deeply moved upon seeing the Master Zhiyi’s *Ritual for the Pure Land*, and he felt profound personal joy.

From then on, he did not dare spit toward the west nor sit with his back to the west. He practiced and progressed according to the Dharma, until later he saw white cranes and peacocks flying in formation.
Descending westward, he again saw lotus flowers with radiant light opening and closing before him. He declared, "The Pure Land has appeared.
Thereupon, he rose to prostrate before the Buddha and passed away. At the time of his cremation, auspicious clouds of five colors covered his coffin.
Seng Fazhi (39): Not bound by minor precepts, he followed the common sentiments of the world;
with a single thought he turned his mind back [to the Dharma] and was immediately reborn amidst golden auspicious radiance.
At midnight the light broke forth; when the cock crowed and people rose, they marveled that it was already dawn.
Fazhi resided among the peaks of Mount Tiantai, making the recitation of the Buddha’s name his primary practice. By nature he was somewhat reckless and did not strictly observe the monastic precepts.
At the Doushuaitai Hall of Guoqing Monastery, he recited the Buddha’s name day and night. At that time, many people did not believe him.

Suddenly one day, he took leave of both the clergy and the laity, saying, "I wish to be reborn in the Pure Land," and instructed his relatives and acquaintances to prepare a vegetarian feast. At the moment of his death, golden light illuminated the wilds, startling the pheasants.
The cry! The boatmen on the river say it is dawn.
Monk Xiongjun (40): Your preceptual virtue is utterly deficient;
though you claim your mindfulness is not deluded, King Yama has already judged that you shall enter the hells.
One must know that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable: a great pit of fire became a pond of white lotuses.
Xiongjun was a native of Chengdu who excelled at lecturing, yet lacked moral discipline; he used the offerings he received for improper purposes and even returned to lay life to join the military.
Later, fleeing from danger, he resumed his monastic appearance. During the Dali era, he suddenly died.
Seeing that King Yama had judged him to enter hell, Jun cried out in a loud voice: "If I, Jun, were to enter hell, then the Buddhas of the three periods would be speaking falsehoods!

The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that those of the lowest-of-the-low grade, even if they have committed the five heinous crimes, may still attain rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations at the moment of death.
Although I have committed sins, I have not committed the five heinous crimes; moreover, I have been mindful of the Buddha throughout my daily life."
He knew the number [of days]. Having spoken these words, he revived once more. A short while later, he sat in the full lotus posture and, riding upon a flower pedestal, departed toward the west.
The monk himself perceived that in the Pure Land, the Compassionate Honored One sat upon a precious lotus; how could this great compassionate manifestation have been without a karmic affinity?
"May the golden hand fortunately come to stroke my head; may my vow for the West be firm and never falter.
This person from Zhenzhou made a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land. One day, as if in a dream, he beheld the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara receiving Amitābha Buddha.
Thereupon, he conceived the thought of raising funds to cast a sacred image of the Great Compassionate One, forty-nine *cun* in height.
Chich established a temple and resided there. One night, two auspicious rays of golden light suddenly appeared. From within the light, Amitābha Buddha arrived riding upon clouds;
extending his golden hand, he massaged Jue’s head and said: "You have maintained your vow without faltering. To benefit sentient beings is your primary concern.
Is it not the same for those born in the Jewel Pond? Ten years later, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, a person...
Manifesting his upper body amidst the clouds, he appeared like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. Addressing Jue, he said, "The time for my rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing has arrived.
Thereupon, he sat upright before the Great Compassion Bodhisattva image and departed.
Chan Master Yongming Zhijue (42): His transformation flourished at Nanping, beyond compare;
reciting the sutras and performing myriad virtues, he adorned his body in wondrous splendor.
He ascended directly to the lotus throne of the highest grade, until even King Yama paid him respectful homage with diligence.
Chan Master Zhijue of the Song dynasty, whose name was Yanshou, was a native of Danyang and surnamed Wang.
Later, he moved to Yuhang. During his childhood, he could recite the *Lotus Sūtra* at a speed of five lines at once. He once served as the supervising official for the tax office in Beiguo;

whenever he saw fish or shrimp, he would purchase them to release them. He even embezzled official funds for the purpose of releasing living beings. When the matter was discovered and he faced the death penalty, he was ordered to...
At the city execution ground, the King of Qian sent someone to observe him. He was told that if [the man] showed signs of grief or fear, he was to be executed; otherwise, he was to be released.

However, the man remained serene without any change in his expression, so he was released. He went to Cuiyan Temple to enter the monastic life and studied under National Teacher Shao, whereupon he realized the essential point of the mind.
Initially, he went to Zhizhe Rock on Mount Tiantai and practiced meditative concentration for ninety days. There, a bird like a *chishan* (a small sparrow) nested in...
Within his robe-bag, he once performed the *Lotus Sūtra* repentance ritual at Guoqing Temple. At night, he saw a divine being enter carrying a halberd; the Master rebuked him.

The being replied, "Only after long accumulation of pure karma does one reach this place. Furthermore, while circumambulating in the middle of the night, he saw that a lotus flower for offering before Samantabhadra had suddenly appeared in his hand.
Thereupon, he reflected upon two lifelong vows he had previously made: the first was to [maintain] his life until its end...

He constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. He made two vows: first, to benefit all sentient beings extensively throughout his life; second, to remember these two vows and further delight in the stillness of dhyāna.
Hesitating between advancing and retreating, he could not resolve his own mind. He then went up to Zhiyi’s Chan Monastery and cast two lots:
one said "Single-minded Dhyāna Concentration," and the other said "Reciting the Sutra and Adorning the Pure Land with Myriad Good Deeds. He focused his mind and set his expectation for this [moment].
Regarding these two paths, there was one who insisted that for all practices to necessarily reach fulfillment, it must be proven by drawing lots seven times.
He then offered earnest prayers to the Buddhas and Patriarchs and drew at random; on all seven occasions, he obtained the "Lot of the Ten Thousand Good Deeds Adorning the Pure Land.
From this point on, he focused his mind exclusively on cultivation, performing one hundred and eight Buddhist rites every day, both day and night. Initially residing at Xuedou, in the evening...

By imperial decree, he resided at Yongming Temple, where his followers numbered two thousand. To those who came to inquire and study, he took the mind as his primary tenet and held awakening as the final criterion.

His *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Source Mirror) in one hundred fascicles remains in circulation today. He also composed four verses exhorting practitioners of Chan to concurrently cultivate the Pure Land.

Furthermore, he composed the "Rhapsody on the Spirit Dwelling in An-yang. On the twenty-sixth day of the second month in the eighth year of the Kaibao era, he rose at dawn, burned incense, and addressed the assembly before passing away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Later, a monk from Hangzhou died and entered the realm of the underworld.

There he saw a portrait of [the Master] being enshrined and offered worship in the Hall of King Yama, whom the King prostrated to morning and evening. The monk asked the presiding official, "Who is this person?"

The King honored him daily, saying, "This is Chan Master Yongming Shou of Hangzhou. Among those in the world, there has never been anyone who attained rebirth without passing through the King’s judgment;
yet this Chan Master went directly to the Western Paradise to attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level. This is why the King reveres him so deeply.
When the monk revived, he immediately traveled to Hangzhou to visit Yongming and pay respects at the master's portrait, whereupon he recounted the events in detail.
The stupa was erected at Mount Daci.
As for the Dharma Master Fazhi of Siming (43):
how could the cultivation of his samādhi have any limit? His exposition of the *Miaozong* (Sublime Commentary) originated from his own distinguished lineage.
He vowed to end his life in order to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), rather than practicing the heterodox methods of self-immolation.
Master Zhili, whose courtesy name was Yuoyan and whose secular surname was Jin, was a native of Siming. He received the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school from Master Tong Baoyun.
He entered the world at Chengtian Monastery and subsequently resided at Yanqing Monastery. His spiritual influence flourished, and his disciples were as numerous as [the sands of the Ganges].
Lin diligently practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).
He once formed a religious society with ten monks, pledging to engage in repentance and cultivation for three years before self-immolating his body to ensure his attainment of the Pure Land.

When the Duke Yang Wen-gong (Yang Yi) sent a letter urging him to remain in the world to transmit the Dharma and save sentient beings, the Master replied with a letter that extensively discussed the essentials of the Dharma, insisting on fulfilling his vow. The Duke [responded] again...
After being exhorted four times to remain, he finally changed his course. The Tiantai school, for ten thousand generations to come, has taken this master as its standard.

He authored the *Zhìyào* (Essential Points) and *Miàozōng* (Marvelous Commentary) commentaries, as well as various records on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. On his lecture platform, he never let a single day pass without discourse.

Later, at the beginning of the year, he undertook a seven-day *Guānmíng* (Prabhūtaratna) repentance ritual, setting it as the occasion for his rebirth in the Pure Land. On the fifth day, he sat in the lotus position and—
He passed away in the sixth year of the Sheng era of the True Heaven (984 CE). Zhao Qingxian Gong Bian composed the inscription for his stupa.
Dharma Master Ciyun Zunshi (44), having burned off a finger as an offering before the Buddha Pienji, practiced the Samādhi of Resolute Action throughout his long life.
At the time of his death, he requested a sacred image to serve as a witness for his rebirth in the Western Paradise.

The Venerable Master Ciyun, whose name was Zunshe and courtesy name Zhibai, was a native of Taizhou. He belonged to the Ye clan. At the age of twenty, he received full ordination and studied the Vinaya under Shouchu.
Subsequently, he entered Guoqing Monastery, where, before an image of Samantabhadra, he burned off one of his fingers, vowing to transmit the Tiantai teachings.

Regarding his instruction and contemplation: At the beginning of the Yongxi era, he visited Master Baoyun Tong and studied under him as a disciple. Before long, his wisdom and understanding stood out preeminently.

On the anniversary of the Great Master Zhizhe’s passing, he burned the crown of his head throughout the morning and vowed to practice the four types of cultivation and the three samādhis with diligent effort.

At the beginning of the Chunhua era, the assembly requested that he reside at Baoyun Temple, where he lectured without interruption. Accounts of his miraculous manifestations are detailed in his original biography. The Master considered only...

To encourage others toward the Pure Land, he composed the Major and Minor Editions of the *Meditation on Amitābha*, the Method of the Ten Recitations at Dawn, the Method of Seated Meditation for Rebirth, the Method of Mindfulness of the Buddha, the *Verses on the Sixteen Contemplations*, and the *Poems on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha*. Other writings are not recorded here.
He lived to the age of sixty-nine. On the eighteenth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Mingdao era, he instructed his disciples:
A statue of Amitābha was enshrined to bear witness to his passing. He was buried at the foot of Yueguai Peak.
Master Shaoqing Shichang (45): His heart was clearer than the waters of West Lake;
He cultivated the Way, yearned for the distant [Buddha-lands], and realized non-arising.
The gentry and worthy scholars together established a society; the name of the Dharma Master Jingxing Shengchang endures to this day through the ages.

This master resided at the Southern Zhaoqing Monastery in Qiantang and was resolute in his commitment to the Pure Land practice. He then pierced his own fingers to mix his blood with ink and transcribed the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
For every single character he wrote, he would perform three prostrations, circumambulate three times, and recite the name [of Amitābha] three times.
He carved woodblocks to print one thousand fascicles of the *Buddhanāma-sūtra* and distributed them to one thousand people. Furthermore, he fashioned an image of Vairocana Buddha out of sandalwood;
having completed it, he knelt upon the ground with palms joined and made this vow: "I and this assembly of one thousand shall form a society of pure practice (*śīla-caryā*).
Beginning from this very day, we shall resolve for Bodhicitta and carry out the bodhisattva practices until the end of the future. May [this vow] be fulfilled."
This is the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya). Having been born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), the late Duke Wang Wenzheng served as the head of the society.
Song Bai, Imperial Preceptor of the Hanlin Academy, composed the stele inscription; Su Yijian, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, wrote the preface to the *Jingxing pin* (Chapter on Pure Conduct);

and the former Grand Marshal of the Imperial Examinations, Sun He, inscribed the names of the members upon the back of the stele. There were eighty lay associates and one thousand bhikṣus who together cultivated the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation at Lushan.
The Shanshan Lotus Society shared in that lofty spirit.
Vinaya Master Yuanzhao of Lingzhi (46):
Thoroughly penetrating the *vinaya*, he further established his own teachings; Guangci received the Dharma and inherited the Lingzhi Garden.
"Homesick for my native land in its pure tranquility, I long to return; having just perfected the wondrous contemplation, I immediately turn my chariot back.
Vinaya Master Yuanzhao, whose courtesy name was Zhanran, was a native of Yuhang. In his youth, he relied upon Master Huijian of the Eastern Tripitaka at Xiangfu Temple to study the *vinaya*.
Later, upon meeting Master Shenwu Qian, who lectured on the Tiantai teachings and contemplations, he extensively investigated the various schools of thought and took the Vinaya as his foundation.
Originally, he constantly wore the *kāṣāya* robe, carried the staff and alms bowl, and went begging for food in the marketplace. He presided over four congregations;

later, he resided at Lingzhi for thirty years, where the assembly always numbered several hundred. In addition to his commentaries on the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* and the *Amitābha Sūtra*, [he composed other works].
There was Zhiguan (Zhizhe), who compiled works such as the *Zhiyuan* and styled himself the "Son of Patience.
At the time of his death, he recited the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra" and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Master Yuanjing of Longjing (47).
In the mountains of India, he liberated himself from external māras; in his later years, he resided at Longjing and befriended Su Dongpo.
Having practiced pure cultivation for seven days without any other hindrances, he immediately departed for the Lotus Land to pay homage to the Buddha.
Master Yuanjing, whose courtesy name was Yuangxiang, was a native of Hangzhou. His surname was Xu. He left home to become a monk at the age of twelve and studied under Master Ci.
Yun transmitted the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai and resided at Upper Tianzhu, where he gathered a vast assembly of disciples;

the prosperity of his monastic academy was preeminent throughout the two Zhe circuits. During the Yuanfeng era, a person from Lishan Gate, who possessed substantial resources, used his influence to seize [the monastery].

The assembly subsequently dispersed. More than a year later, when that individual reported the dispersal to the court, the Emperor again ordered the Master to reside there, and the assembly gathered once more. (3)
When his years had passed, he resided at Longjing (Dragon Well) on the Southern Mountains.
Renowned scholars of the court, such as Zhao Qingxian Gong Bian, Su Wenzhong Gong Shi and his brother Zhe, as well as Wei Mi, Tai Guan, and others, all became his friends beyond the secular world.
As he approached the end of his life, he entered Fangyuan Temple and sat in solemn meditation. He dismissed his guests and summoned Chanliaozi, telling him: "I am pure..."

When his karma was about to be fulfilled and seven days had passed without obstacle, his vow was accomplished. On the seventh day, he spoke a verse to the assembly and passed away while lying on his right side;
he was known as the Dharma Master Biancai.
Dharma Master Zhìyuán of Gushān (48):
Proclaiming the Way through his writings, he was a paragon among monks; sitting alone on Gushān, his practice was even loftier.
He would never decline the labor of annotating the Buddhist scriptures, so that all sentient beings might open their eyes of wisdom.
Dharma Master Zhìyuán styled himself Zhōngyōngzǐ. He studied the teachings of the Tiantai school under Master Yuánqīng of Fèngxiān.
Residing on Gūshān in West Lake, he was a neighbor and friend of Lín Hèjìng. He annotated texts and did not neglect his studies even while ill.

He applied himself with particular diligence to the teachings of Amitābha. Consequently, he composed a commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra* along with the *Xīzī Chāo* (Excerpts for Western Aid) to inspire future generations.
Upon his death, his body was interred within two earthenware jars. A stone monument was erected to record his name, dates, and year;
he did not seek an inscription from those in high office to flatter himself with empty praise. This master was a precept disciple of [Master] Yu. Thus he was buried.

Fifteen years later, after heavy rains had caused a mountain slope to collapse, they opened the earthenware vessel and found that his physical body remained undecayed, though his nails and hair had grown long.

They then dressed him in new robes, scattered various powdered incenses over him, and reinterred him. In the second year of the Chongning era, he was posthumously granted the title of Dharma-Wisdom (Fahui) Great Master.
Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai (49): Having moved through five renowned monasteries, he gathered the most eminent and wise; he cultivated the Pure Land while remaining unimpeded in Chan meditation.
Raising his fist and pushing away his pillow, he passed away; upon the jeweled lotus pond, a blue lotus blossomed.

Master Yihuai was a native of Leqing, Wenzhou. His father made his living as a fisherman. When Yihuai was young, he would sit at the stern of the boat following his father; whenever his father caught a fish, he would give it to Yihuai.
Unable to bear the thought of skewering it, Yihuai would secretly cast it into the river. His father grew angry and beat and scolded him, yet Yihuai took pleasure in it without regret.
He subsequently took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life, relying on a monk at Jingde Temple. During the Tianzheng era, he sat for the examination.
He received ordination and received the Dharma from Chan Master Cui-feng Xian. He presided over five monasteries in succession;

in his later years, he resided at Xi-shan Hermitage in Chizhou, where he exhorted people to practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation). He composed the "Discourse on Exhorting the Cultivation of the Pure Land.
On the evening of his passing, his disciple Zhi-cai asked, "The brick stupa is now complete; what is the ultimate matter? Huai raised his fist to show him and pushed aside his pillow.
Gone. Chan Master Yuanzhao Zongben (50):
Within the Yanhe Hall he expounded the vehicle of the school; the Sovereign called him a monk of merit and wisdom.
When his retribution was exhausted, he returned to the West and ascended to the Highest Grade;

not only did his name continue to transmit the lamp, but he was the Chan Master whose style name was Zongben. He was a native of Changzhou. His nature was straightforward and he lacked youthful artifice. His appearance was full and dignified, and his speech was free from frivolous elaboration.
From an early age, he applied himself to diligent practice and, upon meeting Chan Master Huai, attained realization beneath his words. Initially, he resided at Ruiwang Monastery in Suzhou. Hang...
Chen Gongxiang, the Prefectural Governor, earnestly requested him, saying, "I borrow the Master for three years to plant blessings for this region;

I dare not occupy you for long. Fanben accordingly went there. Not long after, the Chan school was established with sixty-four monasteries at the Xiangguo Temple, and an imperial decree summoned Fanben to reside at Huilin Monastery.
He was summoned for an audience at the Yanhe Hall; upon his departure, the Emperor personally saw him off and said:
Those around him said, "He is truly a monk of wisdom and virtue. In his old age, he resided at Lingyan Mountain, where he shut his door and practiced the Pure Land teachings in secret.
Once, while Master Xi was traveling spiritually through the Pure Land, he saw a lotus seat and asked the inhabitants of that land, "Whose seat is this?
They replied, "It is the seat of the monk Zongben from the Great Song Dynasty. On the day of Jiazi in the twelfth month of the second year of the Yuánfú era, he bathed...

After bathing, he informed the assembly that he was sleeping on his right side as if in a deep slumber. When they shook him, he had already passed away. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa at Lingyan.
This concludes the biography of Chan Master Huanglong Wuxin (51).
Having already penetrated the three barriers, he succeeded Huanglong; maintaining mindfulness of the Western Pure Land, he further applied his efforts.
Thus it may be said that he possessed both Chan and Pure Land practice, appearing even more majestic and formidable than a rabbit with horns.
Master Wuxin was outstanding among his peers from his youth for his sense of integrity and principle; he enjoyed confronting others directly. Initially, he visited Xie Xianxiu at Tie Mountain.
His face did not accord with [the master’s] expectations. He next visited Chan Master Zongjue of Huanglong, where he attained great enlightenment regarding the profound essence of the teachings.
