He styled himself the "Old Man of Death-Mind" (Sīxīn Sǒu) and inscribed his dwelling as the "Death-Mind Chamber. He subsequently resided at Huanglong, where the monastic community flourished greatly; yet, he remained single-mindedly devoted to the practice of Pure Land.
There is an essay titled "Exhortation to Mindfulness of the Buddha" (*Nianfo wen*). Its explanations are concise, direct, and essential; reading it moves one to a sense of urgency and inspires faith.
One can certainly know that its author has profoundly grasped the essential meaning of the Pure Land teachings.
Chan Master Shuben Datong (52): His solemn presence before the assembly is as majestic as a mountain; his reputation for the Way spreads far and wide throughout the world.
It is no empty claim that he inherited the legacy of Yuanzhao; one must know that he followed in his footsteps toward Xiqian.
Chan Master Shanben’s secular surname was Dong; he was a descendant of Dong Zhongshu of the Han dynasty.

His ancestors lived in Zhongshu Village in Dakang, but later they moved to Ying, where he subsequently became a native of that region. He was extensively versed in both Buddhist and Confucian classics and maintained a life of pure cultivation.

Having attended upon Master Yuanzhao Ben and sitting in meditation with Master Zuo Ding, he was uniquely able to perceive the essence of their teachings and intuitively grasp their profound meaning. At that time, his contemporaries all ranked him among the foremost.

Later, he resided at Jingci Monastery, succeeding Yuanzhao on the abbot’s seat. The assembly gathered like clouds, and he was popularly known as "Daoben" (the Senior Ben) and "Xiaoben" (the Junior Ben).
Emperors Shen and Xiaotian heard of his reputation and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Fayun Monastery in the Capital, bestowing upon him the title Chan Master Datong.
Wherever he went, he would not dare to sit before standing images of Buddhas or Bodhisattvas. He did not eat any food prepared with fish or meat, strictly observing these prohibitions.
His mind was free from transgression, and he devoted himself exclusively to pure karma; indeed, there was a source for this.
At the time of his passing, a brilliant radiance blazed intensely. Chan Master Zongze of Changlu (53):
He was renowned by all for his mastery of both Chan and doctrinal teachings. In this supreme Lotus Assembly, may you exert your full merit.
Those who come after wish to repay the virtue of their parents' arduous toil; in their practice, they must follow the "Treatise on Encouraging Filial Piety.
Master Wen-zé of the Chan school was titled Cíjué. He resided at Changlú Monastery in Zhēnzhōu. His realization of Chan principles was profound and his vows were all the more deep.
Yet, being earnestly diligent in transforming sentient beings, he followed the regulations of Mount Lú and established the "Excellence Assembly of the Lotus," encouraging others to practice.

The Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation: Its method is to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha daily—whether a hundred times, a thousand times, or ten thousand times—and dedicate the merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land.
One should record each day’s count using the ten characters (for numbers) beneath the respective date. There is a work titled *Record of the Supreme Assembly of Lotus Flowers*.
One night, Tanze dreamed of a man wearing a black cap and white robes who appeared to be quite young and possessed a refined and handsome countenance.

The man bowed and addressed Tanze, saying, "I wish to enter your assembly for Amitābha; I beg you to write down my name. Tanze then took up his register and, holding his pen, asked, "What is your name?
The man in white replied, "My name is Huìpǔ (Universal Benefit). Once Tanze had written it down, the man spoke again, "My elder brother has also previously ascended [to the Pure Land]."
Fazhe asked, "What is your elder brother's name? He replied, "My elder brother’s name is Samantabhadra. Thereupon, the layman vanished.

Fazhe woke up and inquired of the senior monks, all of whom said that in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātunirgama-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, there are two great bodhisattvas by these names.

Jie believed that when a son of the Buddha performs the deeds of a Buddha, there must be the hidden assistance of sages and worthies; therefore, he recorded [these works] with two great Bodhisattvas at their head.

Within the *Weijiang ji* (Wheeler River Collection), there are one hundred and twenty "Exhortations to Filial Piety" (*quanxiao wen*), most of which teach people to exhort their parents to practice the Pure Land as a form of transcendental filial piety. Master Lingzhi Zhao praised it as the foremost work of the recent era.
Mahayana Master: This is indeed so. Chan Master Zhenxie Qingliao (54):
The various masters of the Dong lineage devoted themselves to secret cultivation; rebirth [in the Pure Land] is truly an excellent strategy.
Praising the Pure Land in successive layers, this vast and wild madman would surely be ashamed to see it—
Master Zhenxie (whose secular name was Qingliao), a native of the Yong clan from Zuo-mian, who succeeded Master Danxia Chun and extensively researched the various classics.
His practice and realization were in perfect accord. The lineage of the Dongshan school reached its zenith during his time.

Having presided over several famous monasteries, he came to admire the solitary and remote location of Mount Potalaka in the South Sea, whereupon he established a hermitage there and lived in seclusion; it was named "Solitary and Remote.

He subsequently resided at Bodai Temple, where he transformed the Vinaya tradition into Chan and devoted himself to esoteric cultivation. He composed a discourse on the Pure Land to exhort the fourfold assembly. To an extreme...

This was of vital importance. The Great Empress Dowager Wei established Song Xianxiao Chan Temple on Gaotingshan in Hangzhou and issued an imperial decree for the Master to serve as its founding abbot.
Not long after, he passed away and was interred in a stupa within the mountain.
Chan Master Cishou Huai (55): Standing tall among the foremost ranks of the Zen groves, How could he fail to cultivate the Pure Land with such refinement?
It is simply because he deeply understands the principle of non-arising; Whether going east or coming west, he is entirely free.
Chan Master Huai Shen received the Dharma from Master Xin of Changlu. He had thoroughly mastered the Three Vehicles and was especially meticulous regarding the Vinaya.

Daily, he held the Pure Land in his heart. At the beginning of the Xuande era, he resided at Hui-lin Temple. He often spoke with earnestness to others, saying, "There is no shortcut to cultivation that surpasses the Pure Land.
He frequently established a Western Paradise altar and gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name. The people of the commandery followed him with great enthusiasm.
Huazhen was a true and excellent guide for the final age.
Bailian Xian was the Master of the Teaching (56).
Within Mount Dongye, he propagated the provisional teachings; his realization of the three contemplations was perfectly clear and his practice was complete.
Having exhausted his robes and alms bowl, he returned to An-yang; as the earth shook and fragrant winds arose, white lotuses blossomed, for he was the Master of the Teaching.
Residing at Bai-lan Temple on Mount Dong-ye in Taizhou, he transmitted the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai and constantly practiced the Lotus Samādhi.
With his mind fixed upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss, on the eleventh day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Yuanyou era, he summoned the assembly and emerged.
He distributed his robes and alms bowl, saying, "I shall return to the Pure Land on the twenty-third day.
On that day, he sat in the gate outside the abbot’s quarters and passed away. Yang Cigong praised his true nature, saying: "The sealed letter left behind, sitting cross-legged;
not dwelling in the white lotus, yet born from a white lotus."
Master Huimeng of Huicang (57): Beneath the wheel of radiant wisdom, he awakened to the Tiantai school;
in his later years, he relied on Mount Jing as a companion to Master Ye, reciting the Lotus Sūtra daily with the hope of transforming others.
In the jeweled ponds and golden lands, his bliss is inexhaustible.

Dharma Master Huicang was a native of Yanguan in Hangzhou. He studied under the monk-recorder Hui Guang at Shangzhu Monastery, where for twenty years he thoroughly mastered the principles of the teachings and contemplations of his school. He became renowned within the monastic academies.

In his later years, he withdrew from public life and retired to Changzhao on Mount Jing, where he befriended the official Ye Gong; together they discussed the state of non-birth and made plans for the Pure Land.
He made it his daily practice to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and various Mahāyāna sūtras, counting the sacred name of Amitābha by the tens of thousands each day.

One day, manifesting illness, he summoned his disciples and said, "Throughout my life, I have studied the Mahāyāna and sought the Pure Land. Now that I have fortunately reached this point, my vow will surely be fulfilled.
He then departed peacefully. When the assembly gathered at Changzhao, they heard the sound of celestial music filling the sky as [deities] came from the west to welcome him.
It remained suspended above the funeral pyre, causing both monastics and laypeople to be struck with wonder. Upon cremation, countless śarīras of five colors were obtained;
could this not be the result of his lifelong cultivation and refinement through the pure Dharma?
Master Zhuan'an Youyan (58): His conduct was like ice and frost, and his mindfulness was single-minded. As music played at the Golden Pond, he suddenly appeared before me.
Those deluded people do not believe in rebirth in An-yang; let them look instead at this farewell composition written at the moment of departure.

There was a Master Yan, surnamed Zhuan’an, whose observance of the precepts was as pure as ice and frost. He was skilled in literature and fond of debate, and he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of Pure Land.
One night, he saw several musicians upon a golden pond, raising their voices to welcome his arrival.
Thereupon, he composed a piece titled "Farewell to Myself. Not many days later, he passed away.
Dharma Master Zheyang of Tongjiang (59): Tongjiang’s excellence fulfills his original aspiration;
Day by day he increases his pure practice with further purity and harmony.
If he can accomplish the ten vows before him, He shall be at the stage of non-retrogression in the future.

Dharma Master Zhai Ying was a native of Fuchun. He transmitted the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school; his practice and conduct surpassed those of ordinary men, and his transformative influence flourished greatly.

He focused single-mindedly on the Western Pure Land, authoring the *Ten Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land* and the *Discrimination between the Horizontal and Vertical Transcendences*, both of which are fully contained within the *Lebang wenlei*.
Metta (60): Having personally beheld the compassionate countenance, my eye of wisdom has opened; how wondrous is the fruit of samādhi at the tip of the brush!
The marks and signs of radiance appear in successive layers, winning a glorious name that pervades the nine realms.
Yumi was styled Sijing (Sincere Purity). A native of Quanzhou, he renounced his wife and children to become a disciple of the Tathāgata, calling himself a "Son of the Pure Land.

Early on, he attended Dharma Master Ying’s lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra* and received the teachings of the Pure Land school. He constantly recited the name of Amitābha and practiced the visualization methods of the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*.
In his leisure time, he would paint sacred images with extreme refinement and skill. Whenever he painted a sacred image, he would first prepare a pure chamber.
He stilled his mind within and called upon the Western Pure Land; only when he was certain that Amitābha’s radiance would appear before him did he dare to take up his brush.

He produced many images of the Buddha one zhang and six chi in height, which were so marvelous they entered the ranks of the sublime. His secular surname was Yu, and thus he was popularly known as "Yu Mida" (Amitābha of the Yu clan).
He established the Miaoxing Monastery at the northern gate of Hangzhou, where he gathered monks from all quarters and provided them with meals.

[He received] three million [coins]. He established ten Lotus Treasury World-systems. In the Ding-si year of the Shaoxing era, he sat upright in his chamber, mentally visualizing the Western Pure Land.
After seven days of burning incense as an offering to the Buddha, he passed away suddenly.
Master Zhongxiao of Shizhi (61): Diligently lecturing on the teachings of Tiantai and Jingxiu, he daily renewed his practice; aspiring to return to the Land of Bliss, he exhorted many others.
Those who are able to cross over from this Sahā world are alone entitled to be called "repaying the Buddha’s kindness."

Dharma Master Zongxiao succeeded Dharma Master Huixun of Yuetai Hall. He possessed a profound and penetrating mastery of the scriptural divisions and exclusively used the practices of Amitābha to transform others.

He once compiled the writings and verses on the principles of the Pure Land composed by various patriarchs of the scriptural schools, masters outside the monastic tradition, and scholar-officials, arranging them into a massive volume titled *Lebang wenlei* (Classified Writings on the Land of Bliss).
It is currently being practiced in the world. Furthermore, it is titled *The Aspiration for the Land of Bliss*.
Observing Master Guan’s dedication of heart, what more need be said regarding his rebirth in the Pure Land? (Master Cizhao, 62)

"Hearing the Crows Cry, All Affairs Come to Rest. Who would have expected that his former karmic obstacles would be dispelled at Jiangzhou? His Master, whose name was Ziyuan and who styled himself "All Affairs Come to Rest," was a native of the Mao clan from Maoshan in Kunshan, Pingjiang.

He entered the monastic order... [under] the guidance of the Master, for whom both favorable and adverse circumstances were skillful means; he sought only that sentient beings might believe, understand, and practice.

His Compassionate Illumination was the Patriarch. His taboo name was Ziyuan, and he called himself "All Affairs Come to Rest. He was a son of the Mao family of Kunshan, Pingjiang. He [went to]... [the Master].

Zhītōng of Yánxiáng Temple left the household life to study and recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and practice *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. One day, while in a state of meditative concentration, he attained realization upon hearing the cry of a crow.
Thereupon, admiring the style of Master Yuǎn of Lúshān, he exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name and compiled the *Báilián Chàn Yí* (The Ritual for the White Lotus Repentance).
Later, he went to the shores of Lake Línshuǐ and established the Báilián Chàntáng (White Lotus Repentance Hall), where he practiced the Pure Land path together with the fourfold assembly.

At the age of forty-six, he resided at Jiangzhou Zanglin. Amidst circumstances of both adversity and favor, he never once allowed his thoughts to waver. He traveled everywhere to exhort and transform others;

there exists a collection of his writings titled *Xixing ji* (Collection of Western Journeys). In the second year of the Qiandao era, Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree for him to preach the Dharma-gate of Pure Land at Deśou Palace.
He was specially granted the title "Master of the White Lotus" and "Patriarch of Compassionate Illumination. Later, at the home of Ni Pujian in Duocheng...
He addressed his disciples, saying, "My work of transformation is now complete; the time for my departure has come. Having spoken these words, he joined his palms and entered nirvana.
His stupa and śarīra were enshrined at Ligan Market in Songjiang.
The Patriarch of the Udumbara (63):
The spirit of the Lotus Society has powerfully restored the tradition; Mount Lu’s peaks stand even more majestic.
Who would have known that within the realm of sentient beings in the five turbidities, yet another single blossom of the Udumbara has bloomed?
The former Master of the Udumbara School was named Pudu. He was the presiding master of the White Lotus Sect’s Shanshe Hall at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu in Jiangzhou.

He authored the *Lianzong baojian* (Jeweled Mirror of the Lotus School) in ten fascicles. During the Zhida era of the Yuan dynasty, he received an imperial edict from the Crown Prince to have it printed and circulated throughout the realm;

I shall not elaborate further.
Master Jitang Yuan (64), who attained the single transmission within the lineage of Miyun,
maintained the Buddha’s Vinaya precepts with ever-firmer resolve.
He traveled throughout the ten directions to propagate the teachings; it was truly a sight to behold—a red lotus blooming upon dry land.
Master Shiyuan’s secular surname was Zhu; he was a native of Huating. He once studied Chan under Master Miaomin Jie and maintained extremely strict observance of the precepts.
He was devoted to the practice of the *nienfo* samādhi, and as a result, a deity clad in golden armor descended from heaven, appearing to him in a dream as a red lotus flower.
He emerged from the earth and traveled through the ten provinces to propagate his teachings, greatly expounding the Lotus School (*Fajiao*).
He universally exhorted all people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land; those who experienced spiritual responses were beyond counting.
He founded Bailian Monastery on Mount Bian by Lake Tai and also established Yansheng Yuan at Chenshu Quisha in Suzhou, where he eventually passed away.
Master Tianmu Zhongfeng (65) When sitting alone on Mount Tianmu, The king and his ministers prostrate before his towering Way.
His meditative mind never leaves the Land of Lotus; He composes a poem on the Pure Land to manifest the mechanism of transformation.
Master Zhongfeng was a native of Qiantang; his name was Mingben. He received the Dharma from Master Gaofeng of Mount Tianmu.
His virtue and character were as towering as Mount Tai and the Northern Dipper; kings and ministers took refuge in him, and dragons and elephants gathered around him.
The imperial court repeatedly dispatched envoys to bestow upon him gold and silk, and he was granted the imperial title of National Teacher Puying. The Master’s wisdom and discernment were unimpeded.
In the intervals between attending to the spiritual capacities of those who came to him, he further cultivated pure practices in secret. He composed one hundred poems on the Pure Land.
At the age of sixty-two, on the day he manifested his passing, extraordinary radiance shone forth. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Tianmu.
Dharma Master Yugō Mōjun (66): Wondrously entering the Tiantai school, his understanding and practice were perfected;
He expounded the four teachings of the transformational ritual boundlessly, Cultivating without weariness until he attained samādhi;
He did not ascend the blue lotus, but remained fixed upon the white lotus.

Master Mengrun, whose courtesy name was Yugang, received the Dharma from Master Guyuan Yongqing. His understanding and practice were both perfected, and his virtue and conduct were held in high esteem.
He practiced the Way at Tianzhu Mountain in Hangzhou; in his later years, he resided at the White Lotus Hermitage on Fenghuang Ridge.
There he closed his door to visitors and devoted himself to the cultivation of the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance. At the time of his passing, transformation Buddhas came to welcome him.
A rare fragrance filled the chamber.
Master Yunwu Shanzhu (67): His practice is pure as ice in a jade pitcher;
Truly, he is a monk of both merit and wisdom from the Su Terrace.
Neither in heaven nor among men do they wish [for anything else]; seeing the Buddha upon the blossoming flower is the True Vehicle.

Master Yunwu, whose name was Shanzhu, was a native of Suzhou. He received his formal ordination at Shanqing Temple in his home prefecture and studied the Xianshou (Huayan) teachings under Master Wofu.
By nature he was lofty and pure, keeping himself aloof from worldly clamor; his learning encompassed both Chinese and Sanskrit, and he was capable of...
Wen was skilled in calligraphy; among the gentlemen and scholars beyond the secular world, there were none who did not revere him. He remained within his closed quarters and did not go out.
Day and night, during the six periods, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha ten thousand times, read and chanted Mahāyāna sutras, performed prostrations and repentance, and sat or lay facing west.

Although he had been ill for a long time, his condition did not change. Among those in the Wu region who practiced the Pure Land path, the Master alone was the most eminent; thus, both monastics and laypeople took him as their model.
His *An-yang zhuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land) and *Gu-xiang ji* (Collection of Echoes) were circulated in the world. At the time of his death, a rare fragrance filled the room.
Suddenly he departed.
Chan Master Tianru Weize (68): Before Lion Rock, he obtained the guide;
Testing those who came to study, he lay amidst the clouds and stood through the snow.
The old Chan master was reborn in the Lotus Realm at the end; do not say that reciting the Buddha’s name falls into the second or third heaven, as was the case with Chan Master Weize.
A native of Luling, he received the Dharma from Master Zhongfeng. He possessed wondrous awakening and profound discernment.
Residing in a position of eminence, he established the Bǎozōng Sī (Bodhi Orthodox Temple) within the Shīzǐlín (Lion Grove) at Sūchéng (Suzhou).

It contained two chambers, named Wòyún (Reclining on Clouds) and Lìxuě (Standing in Snow), where the Chan Master sat daily. Officials, elders, the fourfold assembly of pure practitioners, and seekers of the Way gathered there in continuous succession.
Beyond his practice of the "single-pointed raising" and "solitary wielding," the Chan Master further composed the *Jìngtǔ huòwèn* (Questions and Answers on Pure Land).
He exhorted others to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name and elucidated the teachings of the Western Paradise with the utmost urgency.
At the age of sixty-nine, extraordinary spiritual portents appeared at his deathbed. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the plains of Shuixi.
Master Zhiguan (69): His moral discipline was as frost-like in its self-possession; for a time, his practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* suffered no deficiency.
Having perfected his contemplation, his consciousness was entrusted to a lotus womb; look upon the stele of his deeds, where the clouds of *zhi* grass rise.

The Master Zhiguan was a native of Hangzhou; his courtesy name was Biezong. His observance of the precepts was extremely rigorous. From childhood until old age, he never departed from the Tiantai practice methods.
He established a meditation hall on the southern slope of Longshan Mountain, where he gathered like-minded practitioners annually to cultivate and realize the truth according to a fixed schedule.
The people of Hangzhou followed him in unison; many resolved to attain Bodhicitta and practiced the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance.

Devoted to the practice of the Dharma, they did not abandon it for even a moment, even while fleeing from military conflict. At the time of his death, he passed away without illness, having bathed and sat upright.
The *Biographical Record of the Venerable Master Renzhizun* provides a detailed account of his life and deeds.

Chan Master Fanchi of the Western Chamber (70) Sitting in silence in the western chamber, he contemplates the realm of the Buddha; The Master’s realization is genuine, his countenance free from shame.
Sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are always in samādhi— How many practitioners of Chan merely know how to talk!

The Chan Master Xizhai, whose name was Fanqi and courtesy name Chushi, had known of the teachings of the Western Paradise since childhood. Every morning he recited the ten invocations to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, never failing for even a single day.
While preaching at Tianning Monastery in Haiyan, he retired from public life and built a dwelling in the western sector of the grounds.

Within that room, he set up a small bed and daily practiced the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha. He once composed [the *Thirty-two...*]... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated after "三十二" [thirty-two], likely referring to the *Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man* or a related work.)
Verses on the [Thirty-two] Marks; Verses on the Eighty Minor Characteristics; Hymns on the Forty-eight Vows; Praises on the Sixteen Contemplations; and Praises on Transformation-Birth.

I have transcribed the *Guan Nian Ji* (Verses on Contemplation) and the *Huai Jingtu Shi* (Poems on Yearning for the Pure Land) of the Venerable Master Shandao, totaling one hundred and ten seven-character long-line poems.

One hundred and eight are titled with specific names, and one is composed in rhyme. Furthermore, under the theme "The Suffering of this Sahā World and the Bliss of the Western Land," I have composed a work modeled after the *Yujia Shi* (Fisherman’s Poem).

The "Jia" (Family) section, thirty-two [chapters], is compiled as a single volume titled *Xizhai Jingtují* (Collection on the Pure Land from the Western Studio). As the Master approached the end of his life, he wrote this verse:
"The true nature is perfectly luminous, Neither arising nor ceasing. A wooden horse neighs in the night; The sun rises in the West."
71. Two śrāmaṇeras were of one mind in recollecting the Buddha—truly a source of joy. When the eye of wisdom opened, their path was unerring;
the Bodhisattvas came to welcome them, and they together proceeded to transform others. The earth shook in six ways, and heavenly flowers rained down.
There were two śrāmaṇeras residing at Kaiyuan Temple in Bingzhou whose names and lineages have been lost. Devoted to the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation), they did so for five or six years.
At the time of their passing, their mental vision suddenly became clear and enlightened; they both saw a Bodhisattva coming to receive them.
The earth shook, celestial flowers rained down from the sky, and they both sat upright and passed away.
The Great Illumination of a Bhikṣuṇī (72):
Purifying her robes and adorning her person to refine her outward appearance, she held aloeswood in her mouth and recited the name of Amitābha.
When her retribution in Jambudvīpa was exhausted, she transcended to the Lotus Land; fragrant breezes came to welcome her—how marvelous!
Daming lived by the West River. There he met Master Chuo, who was lecturing on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Daming immediately made a vow to be reborn there.
Whenever he practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name, he would first put on clean robes and hold aloeswood incense in his mouth.

At the time of his death, the assembly saw light filling the room and smelled the fragrance of aloeswood. Everyone marveled at this; the cause and effect of the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) were as vividly manifest as this.
Is this not something one should believe? The nun Jingzhen (73),
who exclusively cultivated pure karma and was naturally free from anger, also diligently recited the Vajra-mantra one hundred thousand times.
Twice he was seen playing as a lotus-leaf boy; one could know for certain that he had departed for a superior rebirth and was dwelling in the pure and true realm.
A native of Chang’an, he lived at Jixian Temple. Wearing a patched robe, he begged for food throughout his life and never harbored anger.
He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred thousand times to adorn the Pure Land. In the fifth year of the Zhuangyan era, he fell ill and told his disciples: "I, regarding..."
Within five days, he saw Amitābha Buddha ten times and beheld the Land of Ultimate Bliss twice, where children were playing upon lotus flowers.
"I have attained the highest grade [of rebirth], so there is no doubt," he said, and then he passed away.
The Nun Wuxing (74): Having entered Mount Lu, she remained untainted by the dust of the world; through diligent cultivation, she fulfilled her vow and returned to the truth.
Surveying the lotuses within the pond, she saw that most were her fellow companions in the practice of Buddha-recitation.
Wuxing was a native of Luoyang. While in Hengzhou, he met the *ācārya* Zhao, who instructed him to make vows and practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

In the sixth year of the Dali era, he entered Mount Lu, where he suddenly fell ill. Hearing the sound of celestial music in the air, he said to others, "I have attained rebirth in the upper grade of the middle level.
How do I know this? Previously, while my spirit roamed through Sukhāvatī, I saw that all those present there who had practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name possessed [the same signs]."
[He] was like a lotus flower. Thereupon, he passed away with palms joined; his body was entirely golden in color. He was twenty-four years old at the time.
King Wuchang (75), during the intervals between the myriad affairs of state, would call to mind the Tathāgata; how many times each day did he offer music and provide meals for the monks?
Realizing that because of impermanence one can never escape [death], he vowed to exchange his dragon throne for a lotus pedestal.
King Wuchang was a great devotee of the Buddha-dharma. In the leisure time between the myriad affairs of state, he said to his attendants:

"Though I am the sovereign of this nation and enjoy every happiness and pleasure, I cannot escape impermanence. I have heard that the Western Pure Land is where one may lodge the spirit; I shall now make a vow."

He sought rebirth in that land. Thereupon, he practiced mindfulness of the Buddha and performed circumambulation during the six periods of the day. Every day, he provided music for offerings to the Buddha and meals for the Sangha.
For over thirty years, the King and his consort personally served these meals. At the time of his death, his countenance was serene and harmonious;
he personally felt the transformed Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming to welcome him. Various auspicious omens occurred, as recorded in the *Wǎngshēng zhuàn* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth).
The three sons of the Prince of Song (76), father and children, joyfully practiced together; A lotus has already emerged from the jewel pond.
The elder son returns to inform his mother that she must give rise to faith; In days to come, we shall ride together upon the Prajñā boat.
The Crown Prince of Song and Wei were father and two sons who all together cultivated the Western Realm; only their wife did not do so.

When their daughter died at the age of fourteen, she was reborn seven days later and addressed her mother, saying: "I have seen the West. My father and two elder brothers already possess lotus flowers, and they shall subsequently attain birth by transformation.
Only you, Mother, alone have none. I have now returned briefly to inform you. Having finished speaking, she passed away. Her mother—
Following his son’s words, he recited [the name of Amitābha] facing west every day;
he was also reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Liu Yimin (77):
In this turbid age, he did not accept the constraints of official rank; relying on Huiyuan, he dwelt at Mount Kuanglu.

Huiyuan had previously excavated a pond to plant lotuses and established the Lotus Society (*Lianshe*) together with one hundred and twenty-three people to practice the *nienfo samādhi*.
Huiyuan commissioned Sengcheng to compose the "Vow for the Lotus Society. Sengcheng resided there for fifteen years, diligently cultivating the practices of the Pure Land.
He once saw the Buddha’s radiance within meditative concentration, and the ground was entirely golden. In the year he was about to pass away, he again—
He saw Amitābha Buddha, his body purple-gold in color, with light radiating from his brow-hair, his hands reaching down to receive him as he approached his chamber.
Cheng wept bitterly and said to himself, "How can I obtain for myself the Tathāgata to rub my head and cover me with his robe?"
The Buddha then stroked his head with his hand and drew his *kāṣāya* robe over him to cover him.

On another day, while he was meditating on the Buddha, he saw himself entering a great pool of seven treasures, where blue and white lotuses were interspersed and the water was so clear it reflected his own eyebrows and eyes.
The Buddha pointed to the water and said, "This is water of eight virtues; you may drink from it. Cheng cupped the water in his hands and drank; its sweetness and richness filled him.
A wondrous fragrance issued from his pores. On that day, after finishing his incense offering before the Buddha, he took leave of the assembly, sat facing west with dignified composure, and departed.
He was fifty-nine years old. Huan Xuan and others held him in high esteem, proposing that he be given the title "Yimin" (Left-Behind Man).
Academician Zhang Hang (78): His refined and elegant character was by no means ordinary; who could withstand his great brush, as long as a rafters?
Having recited the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī one hundred thousand times, at the end of his life he departed for the Western Paradise according to his wish.
Zhang Hang had placed his faith in the Buddha throughout his life. He vowed to recite the Great Compassion Mantra one hundred thousand times, aspiring to be reborn in the Western Pure Land.
At the age of sixty, he suddenly fell ill. He focused his mind solely on Amitābha Buddha and said to his family members:
"The Western Pure Land has always been right here in the western wing of our hall. Amitābha Buddha sits upon a lotus flower, and I, your father, shall be in the lotus pond."
They prostrated before the Buddha and played upon the sands of the pond. Having spoken thus, after a long while, they suddenly passed away.
The elder was the grandfather and the child was his grandson; he had only been three years old when he died.
Geng Xin, Layman (79): Dwelling in leisure within forest valleys in his later years, he performed his liturgical recitations throughout the six periods of the day and prepared lotus seeds in advance.
People say that Master Shangxing has departed, yet he leaves behind a pure name that illuminates the annals.
Liang Gengxin, style name Yanbao, was a native of Xinye. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted, possessing a comprehensive mastery of the classics and histories.

By nature, he delighted in forests and springs; his ten-mu estate was half occupied by mountains and ponds. He lived on vegetarian food and wore plain cloth garments, never engaging in worldly business.

When Emperor Wu raised his army, Gengxin was appointed as Secretary to the Administration for the Pacification of the West. Later, during the Putong era, an imperial decree appointed him as Palace Attendant (Huangmen Silang), positions he declined to accept in both cases.
In his later years, he followed the Buddhist teachings and established a *dōjō* within his residence. He performed prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day.

One night, late in the evening, he suddenly saw a Daoist practitioner who called himself Master Yuan (*Yuàngōng*). His appearance and demeanor were exceptionally refined. The practitioner addressed Huīxīn as "Master Shangxiáng" (*Shàngxíng Xiānshēng*), bestowed incense upon him, and departed.
Four years later, Master Yuan returned and said, "You may not remain here much longer. Having finished speaking, he passed away. [Huīxīn died] at the age of seventy.
18. The entire household heard a voice in the air proclaiming, "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha.
Emperor Wu revered him and posthumously conferred upon him the title of "Retired Scholar of Upright Integrity" (Zhenjie Chushi). This is recorded in the *Nanshi*.
Song Man (eighty years old), though he had not yet fully realized that the pure land is but mind-only, was diligent in his mindfulness of the Buddha and his vows were profound.
He counted beans until they filled thirty pecks; at the moment of his death, the three holy ones appeared before him in person.
Sòng Mǎn of Chángzhōu turned his heart in sincerity toward the Western Paradise. He used beans as a measure, reciting the Buddha’s name until he had reached thirty *shí*.

At the time of the celebratory offering, he distributed them to those partaking in the feast. Amitābha, Guānyīn, and Shìzhì appeared transformed into three men, their appearances haggard and emaciated.

He himself said, "I am begging for alms. He replied, "My disciple wishes to be reborn in the Western Paradise; there is nothing further to doubt. Your coming to beg for alms deeply accords with my own heart's desire.
After the midday meal, he passed away. Only the sound of celestial flowers and a wondrous fragrance was heard as he departed through the air.
This occurred in the ninth month of the eighth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
Huang Daitie (81): When reciting the Buddha’s name, his voice never ceased for a moment; his fragrant name has already been inscribed upon the blue lotus.
You should know that this single piece of Binzhou iron was not forged through the application of human effort.
Huang Daitie was a native of Tanzhou. Originally a military artisan, he made his living by forging iron. He constantly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha.
One day, without any illness, he entrusted a neighbor to write a verse for him, which said: "Day and night, the rhythmic clanging; through long smelting, it becomes steel."
The Great Peace was drawing near; I went to the West and immediately passed away through transformation. From that time on, many people in Hunan took up the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name.
The Elder of Fenyang (aged eighty-two):
In my old age, I serve the Buddha, fearing that [my worldly life] must now end; Within the mountains of Farina, I maintain a state of profound stillness.
With a single thought, one can transcend and depart; do not worry that the road of a hundred thousand *li* is far and long.
The Elder of Fenyang, during the fifth year of the Zhenguan era, borrowed an empty room at Mount Farin to stay overnight. He constantly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha.
At the time of his death, a great light shone everywhere, and he passed away facing west. People saw him riding [upon a lotus].
He departed upon a lotus pedestal.
(83) Zhang Kui, who made his living selling chickens, was no virtuous person; yet as form and shadow follow one another, how could retribution not come?
One must not fail to invoke the Buddha’s name at the time of death. Baochi (Jewel Pond) was from Tongzhou;
he made his living by selling chickens. In the ninth year of the Yonghui era, as he was approaching death, he saw a flock of chickens gathering to the south of his house.
Suddenly, a man dressed in crimson and black robes appeared, driving the chickens while shouting, "Tuo! Tuo! The chickens then swarmed upward from all four directions.
He pecked at himself until both eyes bled; he cried out in agony upon his bed. At the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), a monk from Shanguang Temple arrived.
He had them spread out a sacred image and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. After a short while, a strange fragrance was suddenly perceived, and [the bird] passed away instantly.
Wei Wenjin, the Inspector-General (84):
His resolve was set upon the Western Land to establish a site for the Way; Contemplating the mind, he never forgot for even a moment.
Suddenly, with palms joined and legs crossed in meditation, he passed away; The room was filled with a dense and wondrous fragrance.
Wei Wenjin was solitary and pure in his conduct. He constantly established a Western Paradise altar for the practice of *nien-fo samādhi*.

Before the Buddha, he made a vow, resolving to reach the Western Land, to practice the Bodhisattva path, to protect the Buddha-dharma, to turn the wheel of the True Dharma, and to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
Within the sixth month, facing west and sitting in the full lotus posture, he joined his palms and recited the name of Amitābha Buddha sixty times. Suddenly—
However, as he was transformed, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, perceived by everyone both inside and out.

his spiritual ground opened, and regarding the matter of rebirth in the Pure Land, all doubt and suspicion were severed.

Zhang Shanhe made his living by slaughtering oxen. At the moment of his death, he saw several oxen speaking with human voices, saying, "You killed us!

He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha ten thousand times daily without interruption. Later, when he was free from illness and suffering, he said to his family members, "I see the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise before my door;
I am now returning to the Pure Land. He then requested an incense burner, sat upright, and passed away.
Throughout the villages, both near and far, the wondrous sounds of celestial music were heard. In the sixth year of the Zhenghe era,
Zhang Lun, the Prefectural Commander (108), together with his wife and children,
practiced [the Lotus Society] without a moment’s respite, establishing a Great Lotus Society modeled after Mount Lu.
"Fortunately, we have encountered a sagely sovereign who personally wielded his brush; from this point on, our fragrant names shall spread throughout the world."—Zhang Lun.
During the reign of Emperor Gaozong, he served as the Defense Commissioner of Junzhou and was appointed as the Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Western Route of the Two Zhe Circuits.

By nature he was fond of the Buddha Vehicle. In his later years, he cleared a portion of the eastern wing of his residence to establish a *dōjō*. He excavated a pond and planted lotuses, emulating the legacy of Huiyuan’s establishment of the White Lotus Society.
Daily, he led his wife and children in reciting the Buddha’s name ten thousand times, never flagging in their ritual chanting and recitation.

Throughout the years and months of his life, he convened assemblies at the monastery; those who believed in the Way gathered like clouds, and the sound of them chanting the Buddha’s name surged like the rising and falling of the tides.
He was named Jiang. Emperor Gaozong favored him and bestowed upon him the two characters "Lotus Society" (Lianshe), for which a commemorative inscription still exists.
Attendant Yan Bangrong (109):
Having achieved success in the recitation of mantras in barely twenty years, he casually brushed aside his sleeves and returned to the source.

Yan Bangrong, a *chengwu* (government official) from Chizhou, was once exhorted by a monk to practice the teachings of the Western Paradise and to recite the *Wangsheng zhou* (Rebirth Mantra).
Upon hearing this, Bō-ei immediately accepted it with faith. Every morning, he recited the mantra one thousand times while facing west; he continued in this manner for twenty years.

On the evening of his death, his family members dreamed that two youths dressed in blue robes stood by his side, smiling and bowing in attendance, as Amitābha Buddha emitted a great radiance to welcome him.
At dawn, Bō-ei faced west with eyes closed in the lotus posture, remaining thus until the sun rose.
Xī started up in alarm and said, "I am leaving! He then shook out his sleeves and walked several paces; extending his hand, he formed a mudrā and stood there with a faint smile.

At the jeweled pond, all vie to behold a single flower bloom.

Wang Ai was a native of Jiahe who lived by West Lake in Qiantang. He once established a Lotus Society (*padma-maṇḍala*) that welcomed anyone—regardless of whether they were wise or foolish, noble or humble, monastic or lay—who resolved to return to the West (the Pure Land).
He invited all such aspirants to join the society. He composed a "Treatise on Encouraging Practice," in which his vows for self-benefit and the benefit of others were inexhaustible.
Later, he indeed passed away peacefully while facing west without illness. Wang Ai’s official rank reached that of the Left... [text fragment].

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from between his brows; the light was golden in color and pervaded everywhere.
It illuminates the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, and all lands appear therein.
Vaidehī said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I now desire to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.

The Buddha then prophesied that they would all be reborn simultaneously in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Empress of the Sui Dynasty (114):
With a vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land held within her breast, though dwelling in the imperial palace, she grew weary of her silken robes and hairpins.
One night, a wondrous fragrance arrived from the void; she immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression in the Western Paradise.
The Empress Dowager of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, though residing in the royal palace, was deeply weary of her female nature.
She constantly meditated on Amitābha Buddha, aspiring to be reborn in the Western Land. When the time of her death arrived, a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber, descending from the void.
Emperor Wen marveled at this and asked Śāntisena, "What auspicious omen is this? He replied, "In the west there is a Buddha named Amitābha; it is because of the Empress's karma..."

The High God sought rebirth in that land; thus, this auspicious omen appeared. Alas! Among the pleasures of the world, none surpasses the royal palace, yet even the Empress grew weary of it and sought rebirth in the Western Land.

As for the destitute commoners of the fields and wilds—the lowly men and humble women—for whom the manifold sufferings burn fiercely and who are tormented by them all at once, yet do not contemplate turning their light inward and reflecting upon themselves: how exceedingly foolish they are!
Yao Po of Shangdang (115): Having made vows and practiced for many years, she beheld Amitābha as he came from the void to welcome her;
she lingered but briefly in his cloud-chariot, having no further attachment, and now she must depart, bidding farewell to Lady Fan.
Yao Po was a native of Shangdang. During the Zhenguan era, she was encouraged by Fan Po to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
At the time of her death, she saw the Buddha coming to welcome her and said, "I have not yet taken my leave of Fan Po; I request that the Buddha wait for a moment.
The Buddha remained suspended in the air until Fan Po arrived. Holding a censer in her hand, she passed away.
The Consort of the King of Jing (116):
Having repaid the kindness of the State of Yue, worldly thoughts have been reduced to ashes; not coveting the five desires, she serves the Tathāgata.
Her spirit roams in Sukhāvatī, which is truly not false; upon the pond, the lotus flowers have already begun to bloom.
The consort of the King of Jing was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yue; her surname was Wang. She grew weary of the five desires and directed her heart toward the Pure Land.
She personally led those within and without her household who were wealthy and noble to practice the samādhi together. The lady was refined, frugal, upright, and pure;
even among her attendants and favored servants, there was no one with divergent thoughts, except for a single lowly concubine who was indolent. The lady instructed her, saying:

"I have directed my entire household to diligent effort; only you are indolent and do not follow the words of others. You are deluding those present in this assembly, and I fear you will lose your resolve for the Way.
You must not remain by my side. Thereupon, the consort was startled into realization; she practiced with vigor and deep reflection, maintaining a continuous stream of pure mindfulness.
One day, he said to his companions, "I am about to depart. A strange fragrance filled the room, and he passed away without illness.
The following day, a concubine of a companion informed the lady, saying, "Last night I dreamed that the deceased concubine entrusted me with her regards.
She instructed me to diligently cultivate the Western Paradise so that I might attain rebirth there. The lady said, "If I were to have another dream, then I would believe it."
That night, the lady indeed dreamed that her maidservant came to thank her. The lady asked, "Can one reach the Western Land?
The maidservant replied, "Simply follow its path. The lady followed her and saw two ponds, where white lotuses of various sizes were interspersed, some flourishing and others withered.
The lady asked, "Why is it like this? She replied, "This is because people of this world have conceived different intentions regarding their cultivation for the West..."
As she spoke, it immediately became a single flower; its flourishing or withering depended solely on one's diligence or indolence.
Because they saw that Yang Jie and Ma Qian were both upon the flower, the lady asked, "Where shall I be reborn? Her handmaid led the lady forward.
After traveling several *li*, the lady requested that her mistress look out from afar. She saw only a single altar, radiant with gold and lapis lazuli.
The lady said, "This is the place where you were transformed after death; it is the highest grade of the highest birth. Upon waking, she sought out Yang Jie and Ma Qian.
Jie had already died, while Qian was unharmed. On the very day the lady was born, she held the incense burner and lit incense while gazing toward the Pavilion of Avalokiteśvara.
She stood up. Her descendants hurried around her to assist with the ritual of receiving the longevity offering, at which point she had already passed away.
King Jing was a paternal uncle of Emperor Zhezong.
Venerable Nun Yao (117): The nun’s mind dwells only on the Western Land;
Her visualization is clear and steady, never for a moment forgotten.
She has already been personally received by Amitābha, And within the solar disc, purple-gold light appears.
The laywoman Yao was a native of Qiantang. In her old age, she meditated solely on Amitābha Buddha, never forgetting him for even a moment.

One day, as the sun set behind the western ridge, the laywoman sat facing west in contemplation. Suddenly, within the solar disc, the form of a Buddha appeared, complete with all its wondrous features.
At the time of her death, a transformation Buddha came to welcome her as she departed.
Lady Guangping (118): Without applying lead-based cosmetics, she adorned herself with natural elegance;
in her daily conduct, eating, and resting, she was entirely devoted to the Western Paradise.
Her will was firm and her strength surpassed that of men; she ascended directly to the Golden Terrace to pay homage to the Awakened Sovereign.
Lady Guangping was surnamed Feng, named Faxingzheng. She was the daughter of Feng Xun, the Gate Keeper of Harmony and posthumously titled Junior Mentor.
She married Chen Sigong, the Imperial Commissioner of the Zhen'tao Army. The lady suffered from many ailments and her physical strength was frail;

since her marriage to the Chen family, her illness had grown increasingly severe. Although she frequently summoned physicians, their medicines could not cure her. At that time, she received profound Chan instruction.
The Master was the Dharma patron for the royal city. The Queen went directly to his chamber to seek a remedy for her illness.

He took pity on her and instructed her to observe the fast and recite the Buddha’s name. The Queen believed this with sincere faith and without doubt; she immediately abstained from pungent foods and blood, discarded cosmetics and perfumes, and focused exclusively on the Western Pure Land.
Whether rising or resting, eating or breathing, her every action was directed toward the West. Her illness was subsequently cured. Ten years later... [text ends]

The next day, he passed away auspiciously on his right side. A wondrous fragrance was perceived within the room and did not dissipate for several days.

It is not only those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha who attain rebirth in the Pure Land; even the sufferings of illness in this present life are eradicated. How inconceivable is the spiritual power of the Buddha!
Zhu Ruyi (119): She embroidered images of Buddhas and copied scriptures without fearing toil;
she exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name and even provided illustrations for them.
At the end of her life, she suddenly departed facing west—truly a great man among women.
Lady Zhu was a woman of singular devotion. Having married into the family of the Xue clan, she was over twenty years of age when she informed her husband that she would dwell in purity.
She adopted the attire of a practitioner, wearing plain garments and living in quiet seclusion beneath the trees.

With bright windows and clean desks, she embroidered seven scrolls of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, chanting and prostrating before each phrase and character three times. She further embroidered images of Amitābha and his two holy attendants, which were truly extraordinary.

The number of those he converted exceeded two hundred thousand. At the age of thirty-seven, he manifested slight illness. When a physician offered him cinnabar, he said: "In one day..."
"I am certain of my rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Of what use is cinnabar? he said, and consequently refused to take it. He passed away lying on his right side.

The daughter of Magistrate Huang (120):
Her heart was as hard as iron and stone, her conduct like ice and frost; yet by reciting the Great Name, she passed away and attained rebirth.
Since the fruit of the Path has been realized, there must be a sign: from the ashes of her funeral pyre, lotus buds have burst forth, radiating crimson light.
The daughter of the Magistrate Huang was a native of Siming. She married early into the Yue family, but upon her husband’s death, she vowed never to remarry.

She remained in her husband’s residence, cultivating the practices for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the time of her death, she formed the mudrā of Amitābha with her hands, recited the Buddha’s name, and walked across the ground;
she then stood upright and passed away. After the cremation, following local custom, her ashes were sifted through the earth to verify her place of rebirth. When they opened [the site]...
In a basin of ashes, a single lotus flower grew. Onlookers gathered like a wall. Seng Hao Lin witnessed this with his own eyes and composed a eulogy for it, which survives to this day.
Lady Li Shisi (121), who had lived as a widow for many years reciting the Buddha’s name—what harm could her death do when her body was consumed by the great flames?
Her śarīra radiated light beyond counting; her teeth were like snow, and her tongue like a lotus.
Li Shi Shisi-niang was a native of Xiqian Village in Yongfeng Township, Shangyu County. She had married into the Hu family and was known as Changpo.
She was by nature stern and resolute. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, her husband died; she did not remarry, but devoted herself solely to reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha and the sutras.
Whenever she saw a monk, she would pay him homage, but she would not associate with others. Seven days before her death, she saw a monk wearing a vermilion parasol approaching.
He told him, "Tonight, on the fifteenth day at the hour of the rat, you shall die. He asked, "Who are you, Master? He replied, "I am your guardian.

When the appointed time arrived, light filled the room, and then it suddenly vanished. After his body was cremated, his teeth were like snow and his tongue was like a red lotus flower. Such was the manifest proof of this.
Tao Shi’s Sixteenth Daughter (122):
Her chaste observance of the inner chambers is praiseworthy; a man in white presented her with a white lotus.
She has recited scriptures and invoked the Buddha for only three years, yet the spiritual omen is manifest—how could the Way be far off?
Tao Shi’s Sixteenth Daughter was a native of Xuchun in Changshu. At the age of twenty-six, she became a widow and remained childless.
Wishing to be reborn in the Pure Land, she vowed never again to serve a husband. She constantly recited the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.

One day, she suddenly dreamed of a person dressed in white who held a bowl filled with water in which a single white lotus flower was blooming; he gave it to her to eat. Upon waking, she felt quite extraordinary. One day, she dreamed again.

totaling one hundred and twenty-one pieces— in order that the spirit of the ancient sages and worthies may be widely disseminated throughout infinity.
In the final assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the Great Being Samantabhadra expounded the Ten Great Vows, which encompass and unify all practices and vows.
There are no Bodhisattvas whatsoever who do not proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood by means of this [Pure Land].

Furthermore, those who rely upon it for their practice will, as a matter of natural law, be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), behold the World-Honored One Amitābha, receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), and extensively deliver sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Thus, is it not the case that the Pure Land is the great assembly point for practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching? — Baizhang.
He established monastic communities (conglin) to serve as a model for all under heaven and for future generations.

Whenever Chan monks faced their final passing, regardless of whether their realization was profound or shallow, he ensured they all practiced the method of ten recitations (*shinian*) to assist them in rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus, the Pure Land has become a vast reservoir for Chan monks throughout the world.
For those of our school who study the Buddha-dharma, seek to understand birth and death, and strive to clarify the mind and restore its original nature, this is essential.
If there were those who could abandon this and yet attain the Way, it would be fitting for all Buddhas to praise it together and for all teachings to discourse upon it.

The composition of this poem brings together many superior and virtuous people in one place; the Way of the sages and worthies of antiquity and today is as clear as pointing at something in the palm of one's hand.
It causes all people to see the worthy and desire to emulate them, so that they may all ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. Compared to the world of our time—
Those who exhaust their spirits and strain their thoughts to compose verses on the wind and the moon merely seek to please others for a fleeting moment;

such things are like the transient blossoms of plants and trees swept away by a gale, or the melodious cries of birds and beasts that pass by the ear—how can they be held in high esteem? On an auspicious day in the seventh month of the year of Xinyou, the Dharma-void Master Dayou respectfully submits this.

I have here examined the *Jìngtǔ Jiǎnyàolù* (A Concise Record of the Pure Land) compiled by Chan Master Dú'ān, along with his poetic eulogies for various virtuous practitioners. Having read and recited it again and again, I could not bear to let go of it.
Observing the Master’s dedication, it is evident that he truly desires to cause those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions...
That all sentient beings throughout the myriad worlds may together proceed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss—such merit and virtue are inconceivable and beyond discussion;
how could they ever be extolled by words? Therefore, I have solicited offerings to carve woodblocks for printing and distribution.
I humbly pray that wherever there are virtuous men and faithful women who see or hear of this, they will practice and study according to it. May this repay [their] lives...
One will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land; of this there is no doubt.

A Prayer for Recollecting the Buddha by Yang Cigong of the Song Dynasty. Yang Cigong was resolute in his devotion to the Pure Land practice and never ceased his recitation of the Buddha’s name. He once composed a treatise to exhort others, saying:
"The Greatly Vowed Sage comes from the Pure Land; yet in coming, there is truly no coming. The ordinary person of deep resolve goes to the Pure Land; yet in going, there is truly..."
There is no going; he does not come here, nor does one go there. Yet, the holy and the ordinary meet, and both attain communion.
Amitābha’s radiant light is like the great full moon, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm and sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, embracing them and never forsaking them.
Within the hearts of all Buddhas are sentient beings; in every speck of dust lies Ultimate Bliss. Within the minds of sentient beings is the Pure Land; in every thought-moment dwells Amitābha.
If one can resolve to recite the name of that Buddha, one will immediately attain rebirth there.

The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges praise this with one voice, and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions share the same intent to go. If you do not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can you trust? Do not fail to be born there.
